IV. THE FOUNDATIONS (1875-1877)

The Houses are listed in chronological order of opening.

1. MERCATELLO (Pesaro). Elementary School - Hospital

Negotiations for this foundation began in November 1874 between the town Council and Mother Rosa through the archpriest of Mercatello, Fr Pietro Tamagni (cf. Lettere 3, p. 739 and L 356; 363; 380), and were concluded within three months. On 31 December 1874 the Mother informed Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, then at Lugo for the foundation of the house, that she had arranged for the Sisters to arrive at Mercatello on 10 January (ibid. L 395) and charged her with going there with them. She was to meet them at Castel Bolognese station (L 9 of this volume). Leaving on 11 January 1877, they arrived on the 12th and were welcomed with celebration, kindness and attention in the house prepared for them and for the work: the girls' municipal elementary schools. The community consisted of Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi, superior, and Sr. A. Carmelina Carretta and Sr. A. Enrichetta Salvatelli, teachers. A postulant was studying and training. In agreement with the Mother, Sr. A. Vincenza organized the community and its services: the school in agreement with the municipal and school authorities, and parish activities under the Archpriest (L 12; 13; 15; 19; 20; 21; 25). On 30 January she left the Sisters, now able to carry on well and honourably as municipal teachers, subject to frequent visits from the authorities, who required quarterly and end-of-year written reports on the pupils' progress and the syllabus. At the end of the year examinations were held "with all due rigour and strictness", with diplomas, prizes and commendations. The Sisters also gave lessons to girls of the town who were past school age. The Sisters were rewarded by their success and by well-deserved recognition. There were thorns, however, because of the intransigence of the Mayor, who, faithful, and rightly so, to the law, wanted to establish a relationship of personal employment with each teaching Sister under a three-year contract; the Mother instead held firm to the principle of an agreement made with her as Superior of the religious Congregation on which the Sisters depended and who could therefore transfer them (L 213). Matters went as far as withdrawing the Sisters (L 219), but through the good offices of Bishop Ma-joli an understanding was reached, with the Municipality agreeing to engage each Sister on a yearly basis (L 225, 226). Later the FSA also served in the hospital. The house was closed in 1892. AFSA, Lettere Rapallino, F 25. FcIC. CsIC: D4, D 6, D8. Lettere Pietro Tamagni, G29.

2. UPPELLO (Foligno). Elementary and Infant School. Home nursing of the sick

The Uppello school was opened at the invitation of the Duchess Agnese Borghese Boncompagni Ludovisi (cf. Lettere 3, p. 731-732). Moved by kindness and charity towards the children and youngsters of the common people, doomed to ignorance for lack of local schools, she approached Mother Rosa during one of her visits to Foligno, of which Uppello was a hamlet, and obtained her promise to take on a necessary and urgent work (L L 9, 9; 15,2). The Mother entrusted the opening to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino (L 19,4), who was however unable to go. Meanwhile the house was prepared (L 89). On 20 May 1875 the Superior Domenica Marchesini, accompanied by Sr. A. Valeria Grazia, went to the Bishop to "inform him" of the new work and receive his blessing. She then went on to Uppello, where they were welcomed with festivity and joy by the country people. Within eight days they were already at work: they had 20 girls, some of them 18-19 years old, and 15 boys. "Of all these pupils of ours", wrote Sr. A. Domenica, "those who know how to make the sign of the cross are the cleverest". It was demanding and absorbing work: school for the girls in the morning, for the boys in the afternoon, and after supper catechism for those preparing for first communion. On Sundays in church they taught Christian doctrine to the adults. When needed they also nursed the sick at home. Mother Rosa, kept informed by frequent letters about how the community and the work were going, rejoiced, encouraged, asked for news, suggested what to do and concerned herself with the problems (L 249; 262; 288; 295; 351; 353). She tried to satisfy the Duchess by sending a qualified and capable teacher (L 377), and the school regained its standard. For everything she gave thanks to the Lord: "The consolation of hearing of the good being done gives me the greatest pleasure"

(L 419).

Cf. AFSA, FcIC. CsIC: D 4, D 6, D 9. Friends.

3. PALAGANO (MO). Elementary School. Needlework School - Boarding School

Wishing to entrust the education of the children of Palagano to a religious Congregation, the Archbishop of Modena, Mgr Giuseppe Maria Guidelli, asked the Bishop of Piacenza, Mgr Antonio Ranza, for information about the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne and whether the Foundress would be willing to send a qualified teacher there. Mother Rosa, once informed, accepted, specifying that "the number of Sisters cannot be fewer than three; but four are sent, one of them at our expense and not that of those requesting" (L 43). On 8 April the Archbishop wrote again and entrusted the letter to Fr Giovanni Brugioni, chaplain of Palagano, who went to Piacenza to negotiate on behalf of Archpriest Domenico Zanni; the Mother, who was away, later replied to the Archbishop (L 71) and asked the Archpriest (L 72) for further information. The matter was finally concluded with the sending of four Sisters. They arrived on 1 June 1875: Natalina Armillei, superior, Graziosa Daniele, Giuseppa De Paoli and Emanuela Zonina (cf. L D. Brugioni FcIS), and after settling into the house they began their educational work: an embroidery school with 68 pupils, who were also taught to read and write; teaching of Christian doctrine and elementary instruction to other girls. The municipal elementary school began in October with some fifty pupils, rising to a hundred after the chestnut harvest, which kept most families busy. In October another teacher arrived as reinforcement: Sr. A. Veneranda Picco. The boarders, two at first, reached about ten over the next two years. The teaching produced good results, as shown by inspections and by half-yearly and final examinations before an external board. Unfortunately a serious problem arose with the school in 1877 because of a qualified postulant sent there by the Mother to test her vocation. After a period of good conduct she began to denigrate the Sisters and managed to get herself appointed teacher in title by the Municipality (cf. L of the Superior Eugenia Gaudenzi of 26.11.1877 and following). The Mother explained the situation to the Bishop (L 418) on 9 December 1877.

Because of the unease and tension that had arisen, she was forced to withdraw the Sisters. One of them, Sr. A. Giuseppa De Paoli, died on 26 January 1878. The others left the following February. Cf. AFSA, FcIS. CsIS: D 3, D5, D7, D 10. F38.

4. ROME. Home nursing of the sick. Boarding house - Elementary School

To the four Houses existing in Rome since April 1873 a fifth was added in September 1875 which, unlike the others, depended solely on the Foundress. It was opened as an indispensable and urgent remedy for a situation of unease and friction between the "ladies" of the Pious Union of Lady Protectresses of Servants and the Daughters of Saint Anne in charge of directing and running the boarding house in Trastevere, Piazza S. Agata, commonly called "delle Serve" (the Servants' house). For some time the ladies had taken a critical and suspicious attitude towards the Sisters' management; they objected to the presence of the nursing Sisters serving the sick at home, whom the Mother had placed there from the beginning in full agreement with the president of the Pious Union, and would not tolerate the hospitality, however occasional and brief, given to Sisters from the outlying communities (Fornaci and little Parish) who needed a change of air after contracting "malaria". Informed of the situation, the Mother, who had already tried in vain to solve the problem by buying a suitable and functional building, urged the superior of the house, Sr. A. Domenica Marchesini, to look for premises to rent, and she succeeded. They were in a healthy and pleasant area, at Via della Lungara 46, next to the botanical garden on the Janiculum. On 30 August 1875 the nursing Sisters moved there with three girls whose presence at the "Fornaci" was a burden on that community. The Sisters, and still more the Superior, felt at ease and free from the ladies' inspections and suspicions, to whom the Mother had in any case made strong protests (L 127, 128, 129, 130). The problem of a house "of their own" was not, however, solved. The new home was cramped, only five rooms, the use of the third floor could not be obtained, and it was too far out. Father Agostino Donadio pointed this out to Mother Rosa, writing on 5.9.1875: "This is still not the house for the Daughters of Saint Anne, because it is far from the centre of Rome and the poor nurses have to trot to reach the sick; at my pace three-quarters of an hour is not enough for me to get there". So the Mother asked him, as well as the superior Domenica, to find "a large house, as central as possible" (L 147,3). After two months of searching and coming and going, the "large and comfortable house, beautiful and with a garden" was found. It was at Via dei Pettinari 64; not exactly in the centre, but at least on this side of the Tiber. The Mother, who had been in Rome since 20 December, lost no time in making the move. On 8 January 1876 she wrote to Onorata Colli: "At last we are in the new house" (L 169). The services were gradually organized: first home nursing, then the boarding school and the school. For their keep they relied on Providence and the work of their own hands: the Sisters made shirts and stockings and embroidered linen. The boarders paid a modest monthly fee. But something serious happened: "The kitchen is very damp", the superior Palmira Grillotti had written to the Mother on 4 November 1876. Within two months the damp had greatly increased. Another move was needed. The Mother, fortunately in Rome from mid-December 1876, saw to it in person: "Now I am changing house", she told Sr. A. Santina So-lenghi, "because here on the ground floor a dreadful damp has come out" (L 279,2). Through Countess Virginia Celani she found a house near the Capitol, at Vicolo Margana 12, which seemed suitable and beautiful: ground floor, first floor and garden, twelve rooms in all. With the owners, the Congregation of the Workers of Divine Piety, she signed a nine-year lease at a rent of L. 825 a quarter, payable at the beginning of each quarter. Having organized the running of the house, she asked the Cardinal Vicar Costantino Patrizi for the faculties relating to the chapel (L 283). On 1 February 1877 she moved the Sisters and boarders to the new premises, which became the "central house" in Rome, and therefore entrusted it to an experienced superior, Santina Solen-ghi. The work prospered. Requests from the sick at home followed one after another. The school was completed with the two upper classes (4th and 5th elementary). The Mother assigned an excellent teacher, Sr. A. Agnese Sismondini, skilled at the piano and speaking English, French and Spanish (L 397, 406). There was no lack of sacrifice. Poverty was always a friend of the house (L 399) and the Sisters worked hard at sewing and embroidery. The house rent weighed heavily on the budget (L 371, 375, 378, 422), but providence came to their aid. The Holy Father too sent a good offering (L 399, 400). The year

1877 ended with a positive outcome, to the Mother's consolation (L 425). The following years were not dissimilar until 1882, when the Mother, having asked in vain for the indispensable and urgent improvements to the house, which was in an increasingly poor state, was forced to request the early termination of the lease. Cf. AFSA, FcIC. CsIC: D4, D6. F32. AD1M, 1875-1877.

5. FLORENCE. Home nursing of the sick. School - Boarding School

The beginning of the FSA's work in Florence was a long time maturing. Mother Rosa had first gone there to see the situation in June 1873, on her way back from Rome, and had agreed to open a house the following August. She informed Fr Raimondo Bianchi of this (Lettere 3, L 144 and p. 731). Instead she had to wait almost two years. On 22.2.1875 she wrote to Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega: "Yesterday it was decided to go to Florence; this excellent Archbishop (Eugenio Cecconi) wants us there only as nurses" (L 44); and a few days later: "soon there will be fine work in Florence... I can't wait to go" (L 51). She entrusted this mission, so dear to her heart, to Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega, who arrived in Florence with Sr. A. Anastasia Cecconi, a novice, on the evening of 17 November 1875. The little flat at Via Guelfa 103, rented through Fr Secondo Griselli, parish priest of Terricciola, was not free. Only two empty rooms were fully at their disposal; the rest was occupied by a good widow and her daughter, who would not move elsewhere before February. She borrowed the bare necessities: a bed, a few chairs and some kitchen utensils. Benedetta lived those first days with trepidation, feeling the responsibility of the undertaking; "it is good to begin with little", the Mother wrote to her (L 155). Encouraged, she presented herself to the Archbishop and placed under his protection the daughters who had come "to do a little good in his city"; she asked for and obtained his help in making the work known among the Parish Priests. Meanwhile the Mother sent the essentials: mattresses, blankets and linen; the two Sisters about to arrive would see to the rest. One of them, Sr. A. Del Salvatore Orsi, appointed superior of the community, would go begging and carry the work forward (L 156). Sr. A. Benedetta returned to Piacenza. With a Superior of the mettle of a genuine Daughter of Saint Anne, the breaking-in took place under the sign of the true spirit of the Institute: poverty, humility, anonymity. On 4 December she told the Mother: "Last night a consumptive patient came". It was the Lord's first answer. The work was soon able to count on generous benefactresses and benefactors, so that from the little flat they moved "to a most beautiful house" at Via Faenza 54 (L 183), where the Sisters opened the infant school, the boarding school and the day school. Going to Rome in November 1876, the Mother stopped there for several days (L 259; 262; 264), giving new impetus to the work with other well-trained religious. In the boarding school, besides the normal curriculum, French and piano were taught to those who wished. In October 1877 Sr. A. Benedetta was again in Florence to start the new school year according to the Mother's instructions (L 398; 400), so that the Institution might proceed with order and seriousness in the two strands of the charism: home nursing of the sick and the education of the young. The FSA are still in Florence today with a residence for ladies.

Cf. AFSA, FcIC. CsIC: D 4, D 6, D 8. Letters of Mother Benedetta Carrega to Mother Rosa.

6. PARMA. Boarding School - Orphanage

Marchioness Marianna Cagiati, who had set up a "conservatory" for the education of girls in the former convent of S. Antonio in Parma and ran it personally, asked Mother Rosa for her collaboration "in the arduous undertaking of bringing up honest girls". She would "lend a hand" in everything she could. So she wrote to Mother Rosa on 29.10.1875, giving her the date arranged with the Bishop to receive her: 3 or 5 November 1875. The Mother, who had informed him of the foundation of a house in Parma and received fatherly encouragement from him (L 141), went to see him on one of those days, accompanying the Sisters chosen for the new work: the Superior Eufemia Camporesi and Sr. A. Benigna Mazzini. Having made arrangements with the Marchioness, who remained the effective director as well as manager of the institution, and having given the Sisters suitable instructions, she returned to Piacenza. A few months later, from Rome, where she had gone towards the end of December, she asked Onorata Colli to visit the place (L 169), drawing on her experience in the world of education. The Sisters also took on the teaching of Christian doctrine in the parish and, as far as possible, with the help of some Sisters from Piacenza, devoted themselves to nursing the sick at home. The work flourished, to the great consolation of the Marchioness, who also took to heart the professional training of several Sisters whom the Mother was preparing for school teaching. She received them in the "conservatory" and saw to their immediate preparation for the examinations and their success in them. In March 1877, at the Municipality's initiative, other very poor orphan girls, most of them without families, were housed in the same building in separate rooms. Mother Rosa was asked to take charge of them and, after hearing the opinion of Fr Tornatore, who went to the place, she gladly accepted. The Sisters were to care for them, educate them, give them a basic elementary education and also accompany and supervise them at the "workshop", a watch factory some distance from the city, where they had to go every morning and return in the evening. The educational work of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Parma lasted only six years, but it had the character of a dynamism open to the pressing needs of place and time. This is documented by the Sisters' rich correspondence with Mother Rosa from 1875 to 1881.

Cf. AFSA, CsIS: D 5, D 7, D 10, D 16, D 22, D 29. CvIS, F 58. Pos. Friends.

7. SERMONETA (LT). Infant School - Needlework School

The request from the Mayor of Sermoneta, Sileno Cavallucci, dated 17 October 1875, did not differ substantially from the many others of this period: "A qualified teacher for the education of girls and two other assistant Sisters". The Municipality engaged the teacher for one year at an annual salary of L. 960 and provided furnished lodgings next to the school, as well as two "rubbia of wheat and ten jugs of oil from some Charitable Foundations". The Mother accepted, appointed the three Sisters and asked the Superior Domenica Marchesini to accompany them. Before leaving, she took them to the Holy Father to bless the new house and encourage them. At 6.40 on 30 November 1875 they got into the carriage and reached their destination at 2 p.m., welcomed by the town's notables and a "swarm" of girls. There was no time to lose in settling in: on 4 December, on the Mayor's advice, the school opened. Some sixty pupils came, "big, small and in between". Spurred by great goodwill and urged on by their demanding teachers, six months later they showed an external board how much they had learned and progressed. The Sisters' days were full. After their morning devotions they were at everyone's disposal: school from 8.30 to 2.30, followed by special out-of-school lessons for girls busy working at the olive harvest or other tasks. They also taught Christian doctrine, prepared children for the sacraments of initiation, and gave them days of retreat, putting them up in the house for their immediate preparation. On Sundays they served the parish morning and afternoon. Their house and school became a meeting place and a direct link with the parish, especially at religious and civic feasts. After a few years an embroidery school was also opened, much attended by young women who, as they learned, made their fine bridal trousseau. The FSA are still in Sermoneta, keeping up the fine tradition of their sisters. Cf. AFSA, FcIC. CsIC: D4, D6, D8.

8. GENOA - Staglieno. Infant and Elementary School

This little school was entrusted to the FSA by the zealous Parish Priest of "S. Antonino", worried about the poverty and ignorance of the many children of the parish in the Staglieno area (in the Bisagno valley north of Genoa), which then lacked essential social services. Mother Rosa arranged with him for the Sisters to arrive on 24 June 1876. They were accompanied by Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, superior of the nurses' house in Genoa, to whom she suggested what seemed necessary for starting and carrying out their educational task (L 204; 205; 206; 208). The following July she added a nurse to the three Sisters (L 215). The house was poor, bare and unhealthy because of the heavy damp. The families had undertaken to pay a very small monthly contribution, but they were not punctual or skipped months. By careful economy the Superior would have managed to balance the budget while giving the Sisters the bare necessities, but the pharmacist's and doctor's bills weighed on the debit side. And yet the Sisters were happy in their "house of Nazareth" and regarded as a "mission" field the two rooms that filled every day with noisy and

mixed pupils, from the little ones of the infant class to the older ones of no more than twelve. In the evening, from 6 to 8, about twenty girls past school age came. Occasional reading and writing lessons were also given to some young workmen. Parish activities also kept them very busy, especially on Sundays. The Mother, knowing the conditions of extreme hygienic and financial hardship that were harming their health and that of the pupils, asked Fr Accinelli to request the indispensable improvements (there was no proper floor and when it rained there was trouble), but these were not carried out, so after a period of waiting in vain she was reluctantly forced to withdraw the Sisters, who left their "blessed house of Nazareth" on 10 December 1877. The bad season had already made itself felt with the usual damage and trouble. Cf. AFSA, AA1M 1876, 1877. Cf. CsIS: D 8. L Benedetta Car-rega to M. R.: 6.10.1877.

9. VARALLO POMBIA (NO). Elementary School

Fr Giovanni Boffetti, parish priest of Vespolate, took an active interest and mediated the negotiations between the Mother Foundress and the town authorities. He was keen to have in his native town the Daughters of Saint Anne, whom he had known and appreciated at Invorio Inferiore (cf. Lettere 3, p. 768-770). He offered the Sisters free lodging in a house he owned and contributed something towards their food in the early period. Having informed the Bishop and concluded negotiations with the Municipality, the Mother sent the three Sisters, certainly around 20 September 1876. School began on 1 October. Relations with the local authorities suffered some difficulty in the first months over the teachers' qualifications. A third "diploma" was demanded categorically and quickly. The Mother solved the problem by getting a young lay teacher she knew engaged; she lodged with the Sisters and worked in perfect harmony and collaboration with them. They were content, even in poverty. The municipal salary, not always paid on time, was inadequate to their needs; food cost more in Varallo than elsewhere, and people offered no gifts in kind, still less money. Nevertheless they prepared a pretty little chapel, decorating it "with things of the very first degree of poverty". The Mother was pleased (L 316), but soon learned that the superior was also economizing on food. She was distressed and gave her a stern rebuke (L 334); nor did she spare the Mayor her protests over the failure to pay the Sisters, threatening to withdraw them and informing the Bishop. The problem was solved through the Bishop's mediation, but another arose: the Parish Priest wanted the house vacated so as to let it to some "soldiers" during the summer months, and proposed that the Sisters move to a country house (L 355). Mother Rosa did not allow it, nor did she accept their own temporary solution of squeezing into just two rooms; the Bishop for his part required observance of the canonical norms, forbidding the Parish Priest to stay in the house, even occasionally, where he had kept a room for himself. She therefore told the Superior to look for another house to rent and to sign the contract (L 373).

The work of the FSA at Varallo P., established as elsewhere with sacrifice and difficulty, continued for decades (1876-1935) to bear good gospel fruit in human and Christian formation.

Cf. AFSA, FcIS. CsIS: D8. Sac. G 27-Boffetti. F 35 (Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi).

10. GUALDO TADINO (PG). Infant School - Hospital

The Municipal Congregation of Charity, wishing to improve the running of the civic hospital and the infant school, asked Mother Rosa on 30 July 1876 for two Sisters for the hospital and two for the infant school, one of them with a lower-grade diploma. The Sisters arrived on 1 October 1876. In informing the Bishop, the Mother expressed the hope that "in their littleness", under his protection, they would do good to that small population (L 244). The beginnings were rather difficult because the rooms set aside for their lodging were inadequate (it was impossible to find even the smallest room for the much-desired little chapel) and basic furnishings were lacking, starting with mattresses. Used as they were to sacrifice, the Sisters threw themselves into their work with love and responsibility. Every morning, on returning from church, two went to the infant school and two to the hospital. Little by little they asked for and obtained, partly through the Mother's letters and her personal visit at the end of May 1877, not only what was needed to make "a little home with a bit more order", but al-

so improvements to the works, especially the hospital, for the benefit of the sick. The FSA won esteem and goodwill in the little town for their spirit of human solidarity and charity, open to all, from the little ones to the sick and later to the "home for the chronically ill". As the charitable works progressed, the little hospital of a few beds was enlarged to 120 beds, and the infant school was modernized in its facilities and teaching methods. For almost nine-ty years (1876-1962) the FSA, with a presence as quiet as it was effective, were one of the most significant institutions, almost the hub of that network of charity which waters, revives and serves life.

Cf. AFSA, Registro Prot. 1866-1881. FcIC. CsIC: D6, D8.

11. CASCINA (PI). Plan for a Girls' School and Boarding School

Signora Anna Micheletti, through her lawyer Giuseppe Barsali on 9 March 1876 and in person on the following 20 July, on the advice of Marchioness Virginia Spinola, told Mother Rosa of a keen wish of hers: to set up in her large house in the Pisan countryside a "retreat house" of devout Sisters. "These daughters", she specified, "will come as assistants and meanwhile will at once see to arranging the inside of the house. Their mission here is to be the education of girls of good family, both boarders and day pupils. The lady also informed the religious authorities of her plan and received their full approval. Mother Rosa agreed to collaborate with this charitable project and, having informed the Bishop (L 223), entrusted the delicate task of setting it up to two experienced, capable and understanding Sisters: the superior Edvige Moroncini and Sr. A. Giovannina Pizzorno, who arrived at the lady's house on 25 October 1876. With complete submission they set about meeting the lady's wishes, needs and orders, even lending themselves to long night-time conversations and nursing. But the lady spoke of nothing else; indeed she treated them like "reserve" maids, although she had servants. About the reason they were there she said nothing definite. "One moment she treats the matter as certain, the next as doubtful... she does not keep her word", Moroncini wrote to Mother Rosa. She finally decided to invite the Mother to her house on 7 December 1876 to draw up the contract, but after a few days the Mother returned to Piacenza without anything being concluded. When at last the document seemed ready, the Mother,

being unable to go to Cascina, asked the lady to entrust the deed to the Parish Priest Monacci to bring to Piacenza for signature (L 289). This made the lady suspicious. She became convinced that the Mother had put her in a bad light with the Bishops of Pisa and Florence, and complained bitterly of it (L 293). The reality then became plain. Any attempt at clarification was impossible with a person who, because of her impaired mental condition, was incapable of a settled will. Having informed the Bishop (L 294), the Mother withdrew the Sisters, whom the lady herself had decided to send away. They left for Florence on 27 January 1877.

Cf. AFSA, CsIC: D 6 - Cascina, D 8 - Navacchio, Florence.

12. ROCCA DI PAPA (RM). Elementary School

The first news of the house at Rocca di Papa dates from 5 September 1876 (L 229): the Mother asked Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega to thank Canon Giuseppe Neri and send him Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi's application to teach in that municipal school. Then came the request to Cardinal Guidi (L 234) to grant the Daughters of Saint Anne "to be counted among his flock". Once the formalities with the Municipality had been completed, with the handing over of qualifications and approval of appointments, it was agreed that the Sisters would arrive on 3 November 1876, and school would start the next day (L 245). On arrival Sr. A. Gesuina Moroni, Sr. A. Irene Carmeli and Sr. A. Fortunata Zaccarini found a most "pleasant" surprise: the rooms of their lodging were in a deplorable state, dirty, full of dust, cobwebs and spiders, with broken locks and no furniture. They made do at once as best they could, borrowing three beds and other bare necessities for a few days. On 4 November they presented themselves at the school. The municipal school authorities were also there and helped to channel the hundred or so noisy children into the three classrooms according to their level. They then went to the Cardinal and received his blessing, encouragement and advice. Among other things he warmly commended to them the town's Children of Mary. Carried along by enthusiasm for all there was to do in their new field of work, they overcame the disorientation of first contact with an unknown environment and the discomforts of their lodging: lack of necessities, cold, malaise, colds. The Mother urged them to look after themselves (L 248), to do

everything possible to prevent illness, perhaps sending the weakest to Rome for a time (L 250; 263); she answered in detail, with suitable directions, the superior's questions about the community (L 274; 275; 296; 319; etc.), parish apostolate (L 263) and the out-of-school teaching of illiterate adult women that the superior wanted to take on (L 296). When she went to Rome towards the end of December she called them to her to spend Christmas together; she wanted to hear from their own lips how they were, what they were doing and how things were going (L 265). Reading her letters and the Sisters' correspondence from 1876 to 1890, one glimpses in watermark the history of this educating community, which the Mother had set on the path of self-giving in the style proper to the Family she embodied: "courage... for this is the time to work and carry out great missions, to win souls for God... courage, blood for blood, Jesus on the cross is all torn, and so are we, isn't that so?" (L 274).

Cf. AFSA, FcIC. CsIC: D6, D8. Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

13. AGRIGENTO. Orphanage - School - Boarding School

The "Granata" orphanage had been established in Agrigento and it was wished to set it in operation by entrusting its care and internal management to a religious congregation. Advice was sought from a prelate living in Rome, Mgr Niccola Di Marzo, of the Signatura of Justice and Consultor of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars. Having known the FSA and their educational work in Rome, he suggested approaching the Foundress and himself acted as intermediary, guaranteeing their suitability. Mother Rosa thanked him (L 185) and explained to him the aims and educational methods of the Institute, informing him that she would send him the two Sisters in charge: the teacher Sr. Eletta Bruschi and the future superior Sr. A. Domenica Marchesini (L 224; 228). The contract was concluded on 24 September. The Sisters arrived in Agrigento on 4 November 1876 and set to work at once organizing the Institute: cleaning the rooms, arranging the services, furnishing, setting up and stocking the linen room, and drawing up the rules. Aware that the institution's future depended on the foundations for which they were largely responsible, they worked with dedication, letting themselves be guided by the Mother and accepting her rebukes when needed (L

252). It was agreed with the administrators to order the "cloth" for the linen room and the school materials from Genoa through Fr Antonio Accinelli. So they had to set about sewing: sheets, mattresses, curtains, tablecloths, everything needed for the house, as well as skirts, bodices and dresses for the little or-phans who had not yet arrived. Many months passed in this way. In July 1877 two more Sisters arrived, one for the porter's lodge and the other to help. By September everything was ready except the pantry supplies. In November the girls began to arrive and the project could get under way: the orphanage with its school, the fee-paying boarding school for young ladies, and the school for them and for day pupils. The official opening took place on 10 December 1877. In more than a hundred years of educational work (1877-1984) the FSA gave the "Granata" great development and renown, with the completion of secondary education, various cultural activities and a considerable enlargement of the premises. They now collaborate with the diocesan Caritas in a charitable work responding to the urgent needs of the times.

Cf. AFSA, FcIIn. CsIIn: D 6, D 9. For Eletta Bruschi's correspondence, F35.

14. CASTIGLIONE dei PEPOLI (BO). Elementary School

It was Cardinal Carlo Maria Mori-chini, archbishop of Bologna, who invited Mother Rosa to take over the municipal elementary school at Castiglione, replacing other religious who were leaving. Reminding the Mother of the commitment she had made in person to the Cardinal, the episcopal chancellor explained the situation and needs to her by letter: that municipal school required a qualified Sister, one as superior and two assistants. Once the formalities were completed and the departure arranged, they arrived on 7 November 1876: Sr. A. Arcangela Casalini, superior, Sr. A. Irmina Picco and Sr. A. Nestore Taglia-bue, respectively elementary and needlework teacher, and Sr. A. Fede Zoppi, cook. The school was near the house and the church adjoining, so the Sisters could reach a little choir reserved for them from inside. School work started and went well; relations with the people and with the municipal and school authorities were good. There was harmony and serenity in the community. The hurdle of the end-of-year examinations was also cleared successfully, to general satisfaction, and in the

two months of holidays (August-September) the custom continued of gathering all the girls in the school every ten to fifteen days for additional Christian formation in the presence of the parish priest. The news of the following years sent by the superior Casalini to the Mother was in the same vein. Over time the Sisters showed the same praiseworthy commitment with good results, but there was some tension with the Municipality whenever teaching Sisters were transferred. Each time it required advance notice, resignation from teaching by the Sister leaving, and prompt submission of the qualifications of her replacement, all within set deadlines. Added to this was the parish priest's undue interference in the running of the school, and there were those who covertly sought to replace the religious with lay teachers. This situation led Mother Rosa to withdraw the Sisters in October 1883.

Cf. AFSA, FcIS. CsIS: D5, D7. Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

15. MONTONE (PERUGIA).

Elementary School - Hospital

At first the Mayor Giuseppe Mosso asked for two Sisters, one of them qualified, for the first and second girls' classes of the elementary school, and a third for "supervising the little hospital". The Mother replied asking for clarification and making proposals (L 188); further clarifications followed and the Municipality decided to set aside the hospital service for the time being (L 191). The Sisters would take on the girls' schooling, but a second qualified Sister was needed. Holding to the earlier agreement, the Mother said she was unable to provide one (L 210). Finally an agreement was reached: the Municipality provisionally accepted the Sister without a regular qualification, and the three Sisters would devote themselves to the school. They arrived on 16 November 1876. "Everyone loves us", the superior Sofia Pasti wrote to Mother Rosa a month later, "except a few bad people who wanted lay teachers". But at the very beginning of 1877 the Mayor, to comply with the school authorities' orders, demanded two teachers with regular qualifications and, since these could not be provided, the school was given up at the end of the school year. The Superior and another nursing Sister sent by the Mother moved into the hospital premises to serve the sick with great self-denial, "win-

ning the esteem and affection even of those who had so fiercely opposed the Institution". So wrote the President of the Congregation of Charity on 22 July 1878 to Mother Rosa, who, however, being unable to leave only two Sisters there, withdrew them that same July.

Cf. AFSA, FcIC. CsIC: D6, D8. Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

16. APPIGNANO (MACERATA). Elementary School - Hospital

Marquis Aldobrandino Rangoni, President of the local Congregation of Charity, on the advice of the Duchess Agnese of Sora, approached Mother Rosa to get the town's social institutions working. He therefore asked for a qualified Sister for the girls' elementary school, another for the weaving school, one to look after the various patients in the little hospital and a fourth for domestic services. They were offered free lodging and L. 400 a year each. Having received a favourable reply, to save time he went to Piacenza with the local provost and the formalities were completed. Sr. A. Eufemia Campo-resi, superior and teacher of the first class, probably arrived at Appignano with the three Sisters in November 1876. School began on 2 January. The Sisters immediately began organizing the little hos-pital, from cleaning the rooms to drawing up the rules, so that the single patient was soon joined by others. The little school, which could hold 35-40 pupils, ran in good order and to good effect. Meanwhile looms like those at the Motherhouse had been ordered, the task being entrusted to Mother Rosa. The girls of the little town (2,000 souls) found in the Sisters' house a place of homely welcome and a point of reference, and in the superior a mother and adviser. The parish priest had in fact asked her to gather them every Sunday, when, free from school, she could devote herself to them. The fruits of this solid human and Christian formation soon came. On 27 May 1877 six young women of the town left for Piacenza, determined to become Daughters of Saint Anne. On the 23rd of that month Mother Rosa had visited and come away with a good impression (L 350). That little community was a great consolation to her in the future too, carrying on quietly, with diligent hard work and competence, the Municipality's charitable works (infant school, infirmary, home for the

elderly). For many years (1877-1958) the FSA earned great merit, and not only with the town Administration. To the people of the town they were mothers and sisters, sowing goodness and charity.

Cf. AFSA, FcIC. CsIC: D6, D8. Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

17. ACQUAVIVA PICENA (AP). School - Hospital

The President of the local Congregation of Charity, Domenico Rossi Panelli, wishing to establish an efficient social and cultural service in the town on rational lines, had set up a functional structure housing the infant school, the hospital and the Sisters' quarters in a single building. On 25.9.1876 he therefore asked the Bishop to recommend a congregation of women religious and make the first contacts. In this way he came to the Daughters of Saint Anne and opened negotiations with the Foundress. Four Sisters were needed: the Superior, two teachers, respectively headmistress and teacher in the infant school and teacher in the municipal elementary school, and a nurse for the little hospital. This last service, however, was postponed to the spring of 1877, as the hospital facilities were incomplete. Two months passed in defining the conditions set by both sides; finally the four Sisters were asked to be there on 5 February 1877 (cf. Reg. Prot. 1866-81 and the Sisters' correspondence). The Sisters went straight to work in the infant school, open continuously from 7.30 a.m. to 6.30 p.m. They also made soup for the 40 children. Every Sunday, in the "feast-day school" for adults, mostly illiterate, they carried out the most useful work of human advancement, and they were also engaged in catechesis and parish service. So as not to neglect their spiritual life and prayer they rose early every morning; at 5 they were in the chapel for meditation and prayers, then went to Mass. They organized community life in harmony with their activities inside and outside the house. Several young women of the town looked on them with sympathy and admiration, seeing in them models for their own choice of life. The people felt them close and stayed close to them, showing gratitude with small but providential gifts in kind: fruit, oil, eggs, wine and honey, indispensable for balancing the budget. The Mother, who visited on the following 25 May, was pleasantly struck by the order and organization (L 352). She wanted to reward the sisters by taking them with her to the shrine

of Loreto to thank the Virgin and entrust to her her daughters and the worthy people who collaborated in doing good, first among them President Rossi Panelli, who for many years kept up a correspondence with her. The Sisters still today do "great good to the town", as the President put it to Mother Rosa (on 22.12.1877), and "bear their name worthily".

Cf. AFSA, FcIC. CsIC: D8. CpIC. Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

18. BORDIGHERA (IM).

Home nursing of the sick - Social works

On 6 February 1877 Mother Rosa asked the superior Santina Solenghi in Genoa to have ready the Sisters who were to go to Bordighera (L 299); meanwhile they should study French, which was needed for nursing foreign visitors. About ten days later she told her of the arrival of Sr. A. Giovannina Pizzorno, the superior appointed for the little community (L 301), who would leave as soon as possible with the two Sisters. On 20 February 1877, the day they arrived, the parish priest Fr Giacomo Viale O.F.M., who had asked the Mother for them, sent her news of their first impressions and the start of their work. Met at the station by an "English young lady" who had arranged their accommodation, the Sisters were taken by her to the house and told that the next day she would take them to nurse an English Protestant lady, the one who with other benefactresses had planned the work and supported it personally with an annual contribution of 500 francs. So began the fervent and many-sided charitable service of the FSA at Bordighera alongside Fr Viale, the apostle of heroic charity, who for fifty years spent his life for the poor and needy through important social institutions such as the House of Providence, later the Civil Hospital, the night shelter and the daily meals for the poor, and St Joseph's home for the elderly; he also planned an orphanage, which was to open almost two years after his death in 1912. He held the Sisters in high esteem, declaring himself convinced that "among the Daughters of Saint Anne God is truly loved, feared and served, and that by their disinterested charity they will help to relieve bodily suffering, and by the purity of their lives and the fervour of their prayer they will help souls even more, appea-

sing the Lord who is so offended in these most sad times" (to M. Rosa on 3.7.1877). This programme laid down by Fr Viale, "the saint of charity", for the many FSA who succeeded one another at Bordighera under his spiritual direction, sums up the charitable work carried on over time and still done today by the Sisters among the elderly in the Rest Home. Cf. AFSA, FcIS. CsIS: D 7.

19. MARATEA (PZ). Boarding School - Elementary School

On 9 February 1876 the town council of Maratea resolved to engage Sr. A. Irene Carmeli and Sr. A. Emma Fioretti, the former as teacher and headmistress and the latter as teacher, at the "Istituto De Pino", replacing Sisters of another congregation who could not continue for lack of proper qualifications. The two Sisters, together with the superior Palmira Grillotti, arrived at Maratea on 3 March 1877, accompanied by Fr Agostino Donadio, who stayed several days helping them settle into a situation completely unknown to them. On 5 March the Institute's governing board met with the three incoming Sisters and the five already there, to clarify the position and roles of each, since the earlier Sisters remained in the same house with complementary duties. The general lines of the rules for the boarding school and attached school were laid down. It was also established that the Daughters of Saint Anne would undertake to give "free public lessons to teach adult women too to read, write, cut out and sew clothes, and to give them sound moral and religious formation. As far as possible they would also nurse some sick people at home". Informed of this, Mother Rosa approved, encouraged and suggested what she thought best (L 325). She sent a copy of the rules drawn up for the Institute's boarding schools and insisted that the Administration increase the number of teaching Sisters. She met the Mayor, who had come to Rome and expressed his satisfaction with and praise for the Sisters. The work began in good order: there were 26 pupils in the school and 46 in the school for illiterate adult women. Added to this was the preparation of "about a hundred girls for first communion". The Mother was sure that there would be no lack of vocations at Maratea (L 338). The feast of Saint Anne was celebrated with solemnity; the people flocked to honour her in the church, where her daughters had placed a beautiful statue given by a canon. At the start of the school year the boarding school was opened (L 423), and the Sisters also took on teaching in the municipal elementary school (L 393; 414). The Mother rejoiced with Sr. A. Irene: "...we shall soon see each other. Oh! what fine things we shall tell each other about the Lord's work. So let us compete to see who works hardest!" (L 414). But an "unforeseen storm" broke over the FSA. A "royal commissioner", who replaced the Mayor, who had resigned, and the town council, ordered in August 1878 that the Religious be excluded from teaching in the municipal school and from the direction of the "Isti-tuto De Pino". The people deplored this and protested with widely signed petitions, but in vain. The Mother had to withdraw the Sisters, ready to send them back later, which she did in April 1883. Their return was applauded but short-lived because of a new problem: the poor state of the premises, made worse hygienically by the cemetery that had meanwhile been built nearby. At the end of September 1885 they left Maratea for good.

Cf. AFSA, FcIM. CsIM: D 9. DA1M for Fr Agostino Donadio's correspondence. Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

20. MONTALTO di CASTRO (VT). Hospital

On 4 March 1877 Mother Rosa wrote to Mgr Francesco Gandolfi, bishop of Civitavecchia, for approval of the charitable service of the Daughters of Saint Anne in his diocese, at the hospital of Montalto (L 310). Meanwhile she urged the superior Santina Solenghi (L 312) to prepare five nurses for a new hospital, "a big one with 80 beds", and ordered them to leave on 20 March (L 313). On the 7th of that month the contracting parties had signed the contract, which among other things set the number of Sisters at seven. The community consisted of Sr. A. Virginia Gaggi, superior, Sr. A. Annunziata Chiodelli, Martina Ghigi, Filomena Pugnaloni, Petronilla Basini, Massimiliana De Angeli and Antonina Gabiotti. Many others succeeded these first Sisters over time, earning great merit in a service of charity that extended beyond the hospital for 85 years. In 1962, unfortunately, owing to a shortage of personnel, the Sisters, now few in number and advanced in years, had to be withdrawn; and it was not easy to overcome the resistance of the local authorities and people.

Cf. AFSA, FcIC. CsIC: D8. Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

21. NAPLES. Home nursing of the sick

It was Fr Agostino Donadio who opened the city of Naples, with its thousand needs, to the charity of the FSA, acting as spokesman for Fr Giovanni Casals, provincial of the Minims living there, in requesting Sisters to whom he could entrust the home care of the poor sick of the Stella district near the Cathedral. In February 1877 Fr Agostino, passing through Naples while waiting for favourable weather to travel on with the two FSA he was accompanying to Maratea to open a house, found lodgings for the Sisters: "A little flat in the palazzo of Princess Sannicandro Sanfelice, who let it for L. 90 a month" (cf. L to M. Rosa 26.2.1877; L undated). Two months later, on 20 April 1877, Mother Rosa went to Naples with Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega. To make contact with the reality in which the Daughters of Saint Anne were called by the Lord to serve Him in the poor sick, to make known the Institute's identity, work and aims, and to involve the most generous members of the Neapolitan aristocracy in the charitable work she wanted to establish in Naples: these were her lines of action. The animating gospel principle: to live in poverty, to serve the sick free of charge, to trust in providence by appealing to the generosity and goodness of the well-off. A pitiful case was pointed out to her: she seized on that "sign" and, with an act of faith in Providence and trust in human goodness, urgently called two Sisters to nurse that poor sick man. He was the first of many. "Now a house is being opened in this city", she wrote to Sr. A. Irene Carmeli, "so think of helping these poor sisters by sending them whatever you have to spare; do you understand? My God, we have not yet been able to find anything, what a worry! There is rent to pay and you know what burdens I carry on my shoulders" (L 333). On 30 April she returned to her urgent commitments in Rome, leaving Sr. A. Benedetta, who was able to carry on alone. She followed her with affectionate letters, advice and much prayer. She sent her a large number of "printed circular letters" to distribute and have distributed among influential members of the Neapolitan nobility (cf. L 385). Fr Agostino, drawing on his acquaintances, introduced her to many ladies and gentlemen, beginning with the Archbishop of Naples, Cardinal Sisto Riario Sforza, and she

handed each of them the letter, explaining it warmly and eloquently. On 7 May 1877 the community was able to move into the little flat. It was empty; there were not even beds or sheets. But the ladies hastened to provide furniture and crockery. Providence began to "rain down". Days of plenty, however, alternated with lean days. While she went on "knocking at the doors" of the gentry, Sr. A. Benedetta organized the community in "perfect observance", as the Mother wished, and almost daily wrote to her and received advice on community life and her work, and directions about requests for other Daughters of Saint Anne for new charitable and educational works (cf. L 337; 339; 340-343; 347; 348; 350; 352; 354; 357; 360; 362; 363; 367). After almost two months in Naples she was able to leave on 14 June 1877, replaced by the superior Palmira Grillotti. On this occasion too Fr Agostino was providentially present, acting again as guardian angel and escort. Meanwhile the Sisters had fitted out a pretty little chapel in their flat, and on 26 July the feast of the Holy Mother was celebrated in the presence of the Cardinal and "a great gathering of noble persons". 1877 closed with the brightest hopes: the Daughters of Saint Anne "make their own way", the Cardinal told Fr Agostino, who adds: "I was (surprised) at how these poor Daughters of Saint Anne, after three months in this Naples, have won the hearts of all, Princesses, Countesses and Marchionesses". More than once the "young Count Di Belmonte" had crossed the threshold of the Sisters' little flat with his sister. Within a few years he was to become the first and most generous of benefactors. "A true son of Saint Anne", he gave his time, energy and himself for the Sisters in Naples, even giving away his whole family fortune and impoverishing himself for the Family of Saint Anne, which he regarded as his own. Cf. AFSA, FcIM. CsIM: D 9. Letters of Mother Benedetta Car-rega. DA1M, 97-98 for Fr Agostino's letters. Pos. Friends.

22. BAGNACAVALLO (RA). Elementary School

The archpriest Fr Serafino Raffoni, in agreement with the town's two parish priests, wanted to found a private school for the all-round formation of young women. He had known and appreciated the educational work of the Daughters of Saint Anne at Lugo. He approached the local superior, Sr. A. Edvige Moroncini, and through her

Mother Rosa in August 1876. The proposal to assign three Sisters was accepted, but their departure had to be put off to the following year because the school was not yet properly organized from the financial, administrative and legal points of view. The three Sisters arrived on 13 June 1877 and were joined some time later by another. The school, with four classes, was at first fee-paying and attended by girls "of good family", who were also given French lessons. In 1882 a free school for poor girls was also opened, likewise entrusted to the FSA of the same community. Mother Rosa took these parish institutions to heart; over time they were joined by a needlework school, a youth club and a girls' boarding school, all run by the FSA for more than thirty years (1877-1919). Cf. AFSA, FcIS. CsIS: D7. Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

23. SPELLO (PG). Hospital

The original plan put to Mother Rosa in January 1877 by the mayor of Spello, Flaminio Rossi, provided for the Daughters of Saint Anne to work in the social and charitable institutions run by the local Congregation of Charity: the girls' orphanage with 10 orphans, the attached municipal elementary school, the infant school being set up, and the hospital, six Sisters in all. Negotiations proceeded on this basis, but since nurses were urgently needed in the hospital, while the orphanage could be provided for the following October, it was decided to take on three Sisters at once, one of them able to advise those in charge on organizing the infant school. The Mother told the superior Guglielma Merli (L 377) to have them ready and to accompany them (L 382). On 11 July 1877 Sr. A. Gen-narina Lovisolo, Sr. A. Carolina Rusca and Sr. A. Linda Dughi, eagerly awaited, set foot in the little hospital, introduced by the superior. They set to work with self-denial and love, quiet and content, and were well liked by all. Seeing the success of the hospital Sisters, the president of the Congregation of Charity, Ercole Dini, went on hoping to carry out the original plan, but could not overcome a legal obstacle: the direction of the orphanage belonged by right, through a competition, to a lay teacher until 1881. The following year a new President took office, followed in 1882 by yet another. The latter, consi-

dering the hospital's loss-making financial situation and its burden of debt, had it closed. The Sisters consequently had to withdraw, on 11 November 1888.

Cf. AFSA, FcIC. CsIC: D8. Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

24. CASTELNUOVO BORMIDA (NO). Infant School

The request to entrust the FSA with running the infant school at Castelnuovo was sent to the Mother Foundress by the provost Vincenzo Morbelli on 28 August 1877. The matter was quickly concluded, and the Sisters arrived on the following 20 September, accompanied by Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega. The agreement was ratified the next day. School began on 1 October with 67 children, gradually increasing to an average attendance of 86. Normal hours were from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.; at midday everyone was given soup prepared by the Sisters. The year ended with a special gift from the Lord: the Bishop's permission to bless the chapel and reserve the Blessed Sacrament. The Sisters' praiseworthy work can be seen from provost Morbelli's words about them: "The running of this infant school is in every respect satisfactory beyond belief. Full confidence in the Sisters has led the people to double the number of children, whom they teach with untiring zeal" (to M. Rosa on 4.12.1877). The FSA stayed at Castelnuovo for six years, until 9 September 1883, since the Municipality, for financial reasons, had had to hand over the infant school to a Charitable Foundation which, by the foundress's will, excluded religious from teaching.

Cf. AFSA, FcIS. CsIS: D7. Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

25. BOVINO (FG). Infant and Elementary School

Father Sempliciano OFM, confessor of the FSA in the Vicolo Margana community in Rome, had been asked by the bishop of Bovino, Alessandro Cantola, his friend and former fellow friar at the Ara Coeli friary in Rome, to request Mother Rosa Gattorno to send her Sisters to Bovino. He therefore wrote to the superior Santina, who passed the message on to the Mother (L two for home nursing. The Mother thanked him and confirmed the arrival of the two Sisters (L 405). Sr. A. Getulia Accorsi and Sr. A. Damiana Giovanetti arrived on 3 November 1877 (cf. L Biagini to M.R., 31.10.1877). On 19 November the canon asked her to send two more Sisters to Pistoia: "All the Parish Priests of the city have been informed of the Sisters' charitable work for the poor, and all are pleased and edified. I trust in the heavenly grace of the Holy Patroness (Saint Anne) to bring the work begun to a good end. Let us join our prayers and She will hear us". The Sisters began their free service to the sick of every condition. Esteemed and loved by the townspeople, they made themselves useful and deserving and were helped by various benefactors who joined the first, the excellent Canon Biagini, who at his death in 1882 left the Institute the house and its garden. This enabled the Sisters to extend their work to education as well, with a free school and an educational and charitable institute still active today. Cf. AFSA, FcIS. CsIC: D 8, D 12.

27. TOCENO (AL). Infant and Elementary School

In response to the wish of the Bishop of Novara, conveyed to her through the vicar for nuns, Canon Lorenzo Torrelli, the Mother on 7 June 1877 declared herself fully willing to send Sisters for the municipal schools. Once the procedure with the Municipality had begun, they waited until lodgings were prepared for the four Sisters: one for the "Stabilimento Cazzini" infant school, one for the elementary school, the third as assistant, and the fourth, at the Institute's expense, for the community's domestic services. They arrived on 5 November 1877 and three days later the two schools reopened. Sr. A. Veneranda Picco, the superior, and Sr. A. Pierina, Sista and Corina gave of their best in the instruction and moral and religious formation of the pupils. They also helped in the parish with Sunday catechism and making the altar breads. Changes of Sisters became necessary, however, only a few months after their arrival, for reasons of health and community matters. Every transfer met with the disapproval of the school authorities, who considered (rightly) that frequent changes of teachers harmed educational progress. This was one of the causes of the friction, la-

368,2). Correspondence then began between the Foundress and the Bishop, who informed her of the situation in a letter of 12.8.1877. Some time before, the Municipality had set up schools (infant and elementary) in the former friary of St Francis, entrusting them to lay staff whom it now wished to replace as their contract was expiring. He had suggested the FSA. Five were needed, with qualifications for running the school and teaching. The bureaucratic formalities with the Municipality followed, and when their lodgings too were ready the Sisters arrived on 22 October 1877. Three days later the school opened. The educating community, as appears from the municipal resolution and the Sisters' correspondence with the Mother, consisted of Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi, headmistress, and the teaching Sisters Genoveffa Molinari, Olga Torelli, Pia Cane and Benedetta Tosi. The school was successful and grew in numbers and quality. From the following year French and piano were added to the regular state curriculum. The Sisters also taught catechism in the parish. Later they extended their work to nursing in the hospital and the attached home for the elderly. Today they actively continue their educational work in the infant school and among young people, and are a reliable social and religious presence for the townspeople.

Cf. AFSA, FcIM. CsIM: D9. Prot. 1866-1881.

26. PISTOIA. Home nursing of the sick

To the two Daughters of Saint Anne of the Florence community it seemed a chance meeting of no consequence, one of many on their begging rounds in Florence and nearby; but not so for Canon Angelo Biagini. Struck by the humble and natural manner of the two religious, he questioned them with interest about their congregation, wanting to know what they did and how they lived. And the idea came to him of helping them and inviting them to his house in Pistoia. After a first exchange of letters with Mother Rosa, he agreed with Father Ottavio Andreotti, a Piarist from Pistoia living in Florence whom she had asked to represent her, on the terms for making over to the FSA a flat in his palazzo in Pistoia by means of a nominal lease (L 401, n. 4). He set out his plan to her on 26 October 1877. Two begging Sisters could live there at first; later others would be added,

tent or open, which led in 1884 to the withdrawal of the community.

Cf. AFSA, FcIS. CsIS: D 11. For Sr. A. Veneranda Picco's correspondence, F 38 (letters 1877-78 and undated). Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

28. NERETO (TE). Infant and Elementary School

1877 closed with twelve new houses to its credit, the last of which, at Nereto, opened on 30 December with the arrival of four Sisters after five months of negotiations between the Municipality and the Foundress. The initial proposal came from a Deputy for the Abruzzi constituency, the Honourable Giuseppe Carulli, acting for the Municipality. He put the plan to Mother Gattorno and put her in touch with the mayor, Giuseppe Debernardi. Three Sisters were requested: a qualified headmistress and elementary teacher, an infant teacher and an assistant. The Mother proposed a fourth, to be kept at her expense, for general services. The little community consisted of Sr. A. Eulalia Valdrè and Sr. A. Teodora Barisoni, for the elementary school and infant school respectively, Sr. A. Angiolina Montagnani for general services, and Sr. A. Monica Balocchi, superior. Reporting their arrival to the Mother, the latter expressed mixed feelings: wonder and surprise at the warm welcome from the people and authorities, disappointment that the house was not yet ready. They were guests of the Parish Priest. Out of excessive consideration the finishing work had been suspended so as to ask the Sisters' opinion. The Mayor apologized to the Mother for this, concluding in these words: "The Sisters have made an excellent impression in the town and have set to work with all zeal and energy. I am quite certain that they will always continue on the path they have taken and will without fail earn the merit of having contributed to the moral renewal of this population". These words of good omen, received by the Mother Foundress with gratitude towards those excellent people and with hope and trust in God, are for us today rich in history. They bear witness to the fruitful good works of the many Daughters of Saint Anne who from 1878 to the present have succeeded one another at Nereto in education and charitable service, becoming a significant presence in the town.

Cf. AFSA, FcIC. CsIC: D 8, D 12. CpIC. Registro Prot. 1866-1881.

PRESENTATION

I have been asked for a short presentation of this fifth volume of the letters of Mother Rosa Gattorno. I gladly accepted, even though it seems hard to say anything new about this woman, wife, mother, consecrated religious and foundress of the congregation of the Sisters Daughters of Saint Anne.

Reading the very many letters she sent from time to time to her spiritual daughters scattered across the world, or those sent to Cardinals, Bishops, priests and lay people who in some way came into contact with her, one is deeply struck by this correspondence. The style is certainly that of her time, but the substance is ever relevant: it is that of a strong and courageous personality, obedient and nonconformist at the same time, a woman in love with life.

Used as we are today to being bombarded daily by an overdose of words that are often showy but empty, Mother Rosa once again sets before us the essentials of a word that becomes action. In the letters we find a constant unity between her deep trust in God's Providence and her thoroughly "earthly" attention to the marginalized and abandoned: a most original synthesis of contemplation of the Crucified and charitable action for the abandoned and excluded.

Mother Rosa was also a great missionary: with foresight and courage she widened her own horizons and those of her sisters to the poorest and most distant countries. In the letters we find, among other things, a reference to the difficult mission of the first group of religious in Bolivia. Today the seed has borne abundant fruit: in that country, as in others in Latin America, Africa and Asia, many communities of enterprising and courageous sisters continue to carry out their generous service in silence, following the example of their foundress.

Mother Rosa chose to live to the full the poignant experience of a daily existence marked by the stigmata of poverty and suffering. On these values she mapped out the future path of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, so as to extend in time and space her charism of deep union with God and total availability to the poor. Reading these letters, we see the Mother's gentleness and tenderness become wonder, strength, passion, courage and the witness of a great charity, to which the growth of the Institute was to keep time.

We live in difficult times. Selfishness and private interests prevail over the common good in a society that seems launched on a paranoid race for material goods, forgetful of the "losers", of those who cannot keep up with the frantic pace of our time. So we have great need of witnesses who remind us of the essentials of life, make us love it, and help us understand the depth and tenderness of God's love.

To men and women in search of meaning for their lives, Mother Rosa, through these letters, points to the lasting values of trust in God the Father, service of our brothers and sisters, and sacrifice "out of love". These are firm foundations that have filled and still fill with meaning the lives of thousands of spiritual "daughters" and "sons" of Mother Rosa Gattorno, and of all who look to this strong and gentle woman to face life's events with faith and courage.

The fruits of the Spirit are always timely, in every season of history. These letters were written long ago. Today they are offered to us again, not only to recall the past but also to help us live our own time immersed in God's immense love. Then the anxieties and fears of modern life will find an answer of hope.

Fr Mario Picchi

INTRODUCTION

This section of M. Rosa Gattorno's correspondence, with its 443 letters, seems to offer nothing substantially different from the earlier ones (1438) gathered in the first four volumes. Day after day they express the journey of the Institute and weave, in the watermark of events and interacting persons, its historical continuity in space and time; they also trace the development of the Family, which was taking shape in its apostolic responses to various calls and needs and acquiring the distinctive features expressed in the "Rules" approved by the Church as the seal of the Spirit. A panoramic view of these two years is given by the two circular letters of M. Rosa and of the Co-founder Fr Tornatore, with essential and concise emphases drawn in terms of cause and effect:

"The Lord blesses us" and fills our Family with benefits and mercy. This is shown by the goodwill of the Vicar of Christ, Pope Leo XIII, who "is very glad to see how rapidly our Institute is spreading" and has "definitively recognized our family as a religious family, that is, a family of God" (LC 1880). "The Bishops of the various dioceses also show themselves very pleased with the work we do there. And we win the sympathy of the people among whom we work". (Cf. L 1). "So many blessings from Heaven come to us through the prayers that our Holy Mother constantly offers before the Lord's throne. Yes, it is through her prayers that the Institute is spreading rapidly" (ibid.). The growth over these two years was indeed great: 147 young women entered the Novitiate, 22 houses were opened, and there were countless requests for further foundations, with expansion reaching beyond the Ocean, to Bolivia. Writing to Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni in La Paz, M. Rosa summed up the situation: "The requests we have here in Italy for the Daughters of Saint Anne are a big affair... In Sicily we already have 6 houses, but they are asking for as many again. Soon we shall be in all the main cities of Sicily, not counting those being opened and the requests we have here. I don't know how to satisfy them" (L 357,3). The Foundress always tries to respond to the many requests, because

the Work is the Lord's; He sends workers into his field. She has only to, and can, on the strength of His love, walk on, give herself, give all of herself and her time, whose preciousness she measures by St Paul's "urget".

Of the many young women whom the heavenly Father sends to the Family of the Holy Mother of Mary, she forms "true Daughters of Saint Anne" (L 356,4) and communicates to them, in person and in writing, the vital energy that presses within her and moves her: "the charity that rules me never says enough, but makes me say that it is stronger than my strength, for it is in my very depths that it does violence" (to Fr Agostino Donadio, 8.1.1875). An unstoppable charity that disposes her to the unconditional gift of herself and her daughters, urging them to a service of motherly dedication "without limits and without reward" for the good of all. In fidelity to the Church and to the Father. (L 1,10; 63,12; 75,3). For, she declares with firm certainty, "now that we have been approved, we are true daughters of the apostolic and Roman Church" (L 299,8; 60,12; 104,6).

She sends those daughters, still very young but sound in spirit (L 403), in groups of three or four, rarely more, according to requests, to places of which they know only the name but which are waiting for them. And the little apostolic bands set out, entrusting themselves to the Holy Mother, to northern, central and southern Italy and to distant Sicily. They are needed. As significant presences they will be a driving leaven of animation and renewal in social, charitable, educational and hospital structures, generally already existing and mostly run by government or church bodies. Others again, the missionaries, go overseas... to America. The Mother has prepared them for the great adventure and regrets not being able to share their happy lot (L 207) and to spend herself with her daughters, living the beatitude reserved for them: "blessed are you who for Jesus have crossed the sea and travelled a fine road so that you can become saints, and what is more, ready to endure martyrdom" (L 311,10).

The distance, the unfamiliarity of the places, the long, inexplicable silences in her daughters' letters, broken by alarming news, the death of two Sisters (L 288) and the very serious illness of the superior Sr. A. Giuseppa, will be her martyrdom and make her heart bleed. "How painful not to have letters from you!" "My God! what a distance, it is truly a very great pain" (L 299; 305; 357; 377). "Certainly, those in Italy do not cost me as many pray-

ers as you do" (L 299). But faith grows stronger: "Courage, a brief suffering for an eternal joy" (ibid.), and hope spreads the wings of the prophesied "dove" for bolder and longer flights. In La Paz the Novitiate is opened (L 377); a young Bolivian woman receives the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne: Sr. A. Rosa Tellería, the first of a long line.

The expansion of the Institute is a considerable burden for the Mother, and the letters clearly testify to her many-sided commitment in her role as Foundress, Mother, Formator and Superior general. Aware that all this is willed by God for her, she continues to plant, cultivate and strengthen the Family. Her presence, even in works already well established, is always desired, and in difficulties urgently called for by her daughters; her letters are as necessary as bread. She does not hold back and, when needed, takes decisive action (in these two years she closes three of the houses opened only a few months before); she firmly and resolutely defends her daughters against slanders damaging to the Institute's good name (as in the case of Florence) and fights for them to remain in their field of work, and with the weapons of prayer and humility succeeds in having the truth of the facts acknowledged.

This suffering and spending of herself is the quickest way to Calvary. Always uphill, sometimes steep and rough. But love "gives her vigour, energy and strength"; "Calvary alone", she says, "I know to be the safe place to stop".

[Dearest daughters,]

  1. Oh! how good is the God of Israel! So we have every reason to exclaim, seeing the great mercies with which he has filled us this year too. Yes, his most merciful eyes have been continually open upon our poor Institute.2

  2. The Daughter of Saint Anne no longer lives for herself but for her Institute; so she counts as her own the benefits the Lord has poured out on the Family of the Holy Mother.3 The chief benefit, to be counted before all others, is that of having granted the sisters, in general, the grace of observance. Among the virtues I shall touch only on holy indifference, which is like the uniform of the Daughters of Saint Anne, keeping them detached from everything so as to be ready for any place to which obedience may wish to send them.4

  3. Yes, to our heart's great joy we must say that in general none ever made excuses for not leaving the house where she lived to go to the one to which we assigned her. Likewise the ready spirit with which they devoted themselves to nursing the sick and educating young girls was admirable.

  4. Yet a little cockle mixed with the good wheat in the Lord's chosen field is to be deplored; in particular we must condemn the spirit of those few who have let themselves reveal their sisters' failings to outsiders. A detestable spirit, because utterly opposed to that love of Family which more than anything must animate our Institute: a love that keeps the doors of our houses closed to parish priests, priests and lay people of any condition, so that nothing

they can learn of what goes on inside. A detestable spirit, we repeat, against which some Superiors, being more exposed to this danger, should have been careful to guard.5

5. Ah yes, in the bitterness of our spirit we must lament that some have been tainted with this vice, not ashamed to correspond even by letter with outside priests, under the pretext of spirituality, telling them all that went on among their sisters. And who are these unnatural ones? Precisely those who are cunning, two-faced with their superiors, who like to keep them in the dark about everything that happens in the houses over which they preside as representatives of their general.6

6. The betrayers of the Institute are truly very few, almost none; yet, Sisters, we invite you to pray that the Holy Mother may convert these strays, or else that, once this bad seed is recognized, it be uprooted from the office of superior and, if need be, from the Institute as well.

7. Our Institute's relations with outsiders are consoling in every respect. And first of all, how the Holy Father continues in his special love for us!!! Among the many tokens he has given of this particular affection, an outstanding one is what we received most recently: he has deigned to buy us a fine House in Rome at the place called the little Parish, where a school of ours is flourishing.7 With what gentleness he continues to receive the sisters when they go to his audience!

  1. The Bishops too have shown themselves favourable; as a token of their affection there were the letters of commendation they wrote in favour of the Institute.

  2. What calls we have had to open new houses, so that this year eleven houses8 have been opened! The many vocations testify to the esteem of the people in general; indeed this year 82 sisters received the habit.

  1. This esteem we enjoy among people in the world we must value only as a sign that our Institute is of spiritual and temporal benefit to the Church. And so that the Lord is glorified through us, as we correspond to the immediate purpose for which he has placed us in his Church, which is to honour, and to have all honour, the august and glorious Mother of the Immaculate, our Mother Saint Anne.

  2. And at the same time it should make us reflect that it is the Holy Mother's protection over us that draws down from heaven all

these blessings, and should kindle us with ever new flames, so that we burn more and more with holy, fervent and filial affection for this our most exalted and most tender Mother.

  1. Oh yes, sisters, the holy Mother is for us the channel through which all graces come to us from heaven by the hands of Mary, her Immaculate Daughter. Oh! how happy are those who are her true Daughters! Having shown themselves devoted9 daughters of this blessed one in life, at death she shows them such motherly gentleness that their death is the sleep of the just and a foretaste of holy Paradise.

  2. This year she has drawn 13 sisters to heaven. We recall the duty to pray for them as laid down in the holy Rules.

  3. Superiors are reminded not to send a sister alone in third class and to send the exact accounts for the year 1877.

God bless you

Gio. Batta Tornatore S. Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno
