affectionate M.Rosa

Warm greetings to my dear daughters.

1 The addressee is missing in the original. Given the Mother's departure, it is thought to have been sent to the sister she had put in charge of the community during her absence.

2 The date is deduced from the context, in relation to M. Rosa's movements after leaving Piacenza on 3 January. Cf. L 2,1.

3 Monday the 7th. She probably arrived a few days later.

She sends a money order to be cashed. Good news from the house she is visiting. Some administrative advice.

A.M.F. Dear son,

  1. A line in haste; I enclose this money order, cash it. If you had seen what I was holding in my hand this morning!! Dear Jesus, what emotions! from Rome you will hear such fine things!

  2. Tomorrow I leave and stop two days in Florence. There is nothing to fear; everything is calming down.2 I cannot write at length; I am overwhelmed with visits and work.

  3. It looks like the house of Bethlehem.3 Oh! how much wine, they sell it; three flasks [are] for Carla, white. The things they bring cannot be described. I want the Motherhouse cash book to be kept separate, and all the other Houses entered in the other one.4

Goodbye, a kiss to the Little Doll and to Carla (and yours). I am your affectionate M.Rosa

1 As is clear from the context and content of this letter, the Mother was certainly in Pistoia. She must have written Piacenza by mistake.

2 She refers to the problems of the Florence House.

3 As at Bethlehem, people bring many gifts for the Sisters.

4 The Motherhouse accounts were to be recorded in a separate cash book, apart from those of the other houses.

Advice about the house. She reassures her about the spiritual exercises and commends two novices to her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. A line to give to the Sister who is to come there to beg.1 Listen, try to see that the archpriest is satisfied, and then rest assured that you will come for the Holy Exercises; I cannot say more; I fear there will be two groups;2 so be at peace, for you will come at the time of the Cardinal.3 Listen, more in person.4

  2. I commend the two novices to you, because I want them to do well; they are two dear creatures, as good as can be, sensible, but you know well that being novices they need to be guided; I entrust everything (to) to you.5

Goodbye, in haste, your affectionate M.Rosa

1 Cf. L 4, n. 1.

2 two groups... two sessions.

3 The new Cardinal Protector was to visit Piacenza.

4 I shall give you further news in person.

5 to be guided... to be closely followed, because they need formation; so she entrusts them to her with confidence.

She tells her of the arrival of two Sisters assigned to open the new house at S. Luca d'Albaro. Recommendations about it.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I received Carlotta's decoction and the cake. I tell you, it is too much! And what is to be done with it? Oh! money wasted, my God!

  2. I hear that Fr Accinelli has had to add 7.300 to the house rent. For pity's sake, my daughter!2

  3. Now these two I am sending you, for whom it is truly a sacrifice: I tell you they are to serve at Albaro; Sr. A. Beata will be Superior and Sr. A. Fausta teacher, as she has the diploma; give them the cook who was at S. Antonio, and so there will be three3. That is enough for now, and later, if they have more girls, others will be sent.

  4. I would not want you to keep them4 to sit up at night even once. I hope you will see to it; write to me in Rome, where I shall be by the 15th of Jan.5

Goodbye, your affectionate M. R.

Send me the S.P.d'Arena books at once together with the letter. Goodbye, your

[M.R.]

1 The date is deduced from the context.

2 A few days earlier the community had moved to a larger house through Fr Accinelli's efforts. The Mother urges the Superior to eco-nomize. Accinelli had advanced only £ 300.

3 Sr. A. Beata and Sr. A. Fausta Torriani, together with Sr. A. Restilde Colombo, former cook of the closed house of S. Antonino in Genoa, arrived at the new house on 8 January 1878. Cf. L of Sr. A. Beata Torriani, 9.1.1878, to M. Rosa.

4 She fears that in Genoa she will send them to nurse the sick at night.

5 The 15th of this January. She reached Rome on 11 January.

She sends a basket; trying to meet their requests.

A.M.F.

My son,

  1. No sooner arrived than here I am, pen in hand, for you; your letter together with Carla's gives me more pleasure than you can believe. I enclose a little receipt,2 for a basket of pine cones and sweet mandarins.

  2. I hear you wanted toys for the Little Doll;3 be patient, we shall send them one of these days. The rug cannot be sent; I'll tell you why in person.

  1. Dear children, you cannot imagine how much there is to do; what I have done in Rome is indescribable, so have pity on me, for I cannot do more. I am doing what a giant's strength could not. Oh yes! If the good God accepts my labours, you too will be rewarded.

  2. Tomorrow Sr. A. Benedetta will go out4 specially for the toys, and we shall bring so many you will tire of them.

Goodbye, your affectionate Mother Rosa

So many lovely things! You will see!

1 The date is deduced from the context.

2 The receipt for collecting the basket she sent.

3 giocarelli: on 13.1.78 Gaspare had asked for illustrated fairy-tale books to be bought to amuse the Little Doll, the pet name for little Maria Adelaide.

4 sortirà: will go out.

She should send two Sisters to Rome. She should give them the 1877 accounts.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. As soon as you receive this, see whether among your Sisters you have a good, healthy one to send me here together with Sr. A. Carolina, who is at Spello.1

  2. Sure of your obedience in doing this as soon as possible, I add only a reminder to send me the accounts for the past year; and if you have no money for the sisters' journey, write and tell me and I shall send it at once.

Goodbye, your affectionate M.Rosa

1 See whether: choose from among the sisters of your community... She herself was to ask for Sr. A. Carolina Rusca at Spello to leave with the other.

£ already in Rome. She will send her a picture of Saint Anne. She asks for news of the house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Here I am in Rome. Tomorrow I shall send you a fine picture of Saint Anne, large and truly beautiful, for your chapel, and a small ciborium too. Write and tell me if you need anything else.

  2. Is providence still coming?3 And what is the good Canon doing?4 Give him my greetings, and the confessor too; the sisters should pray for my intention.

Goodbye, your affectionate M.Rosa

1 This and several other letters were catalogued as addressed to Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi. However, she went to Pistoia from Rome on 28 October 1878 to replace Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, who was to leave for America. Cf. Troni's L of the same date to M.Rosa. Evidently Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni had left these letters in Pistoia and they were kept by Sr. A. Crocifissa.

2 The date is deduced from the context.

3 Providence was abundant because the people of Pistoia felt deep gratitude to the Sisters, loved and esteemed by all for their dedication to the sick, rich and poor alike.

4 Canon Angelo Biagini, the benefactor who had offered the FSA a flat in his house. Cf. Lettere 4, p. 679.

She invites her to come to her for treatment. Leave for a month's absence will be asked of the Municipality.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear you are not too well. Come here to me at once in the same carriage I have ordered; don't delay. Obey, and so you will recover here. I did the same with another teacher who soon recovered.

  2. So a month's leave will be requested1, and then the cold will pass and you will be well. Your health matters too much to me, and surely it will matter to the town council too,2 and you will return healthy. I expect you tomorrow evening.

Goodbye, your affectionate M.Rosa

1 The school authorities' approval was needed for her to be absent, since the Sister was headmistress and teacher of the municipal school at Rocca di Papa. 2 Your health will surely matter to the municipal authorities too.

2 Your health will surely be of concern to the municipal authorities too.

She assigns three new Sisters to her community. She regrets that she sent two Sisters she had sent her earlier to the Sestri house; they must be brought back to Genoa.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Three sisters will arrive: Sr. A. Ermana, Sr. A. Mansueta and Sr. A. Fedele.1 Listen, I am very sorry that you sent those two sisters to Sestri.2 You know that when I handed them over to you I said: "Mind you don't let them out of your sight; I am entrusting them to you because I see you really want them, but be careful not to do otherwise", and you sent them to Sestri! Dear daughter, if you knew how distressed I am!3

  2. Enough; please send me a line at once to say you have made the change; send them Sr. A. Mansueta and take Sr. A. Felicita back at once, at once; you can leave them the other for a while, then I shall soon send another and you will take Sr. A. Berarda back again. Do you understand?

  3. I hope that when this reaches you, you will already have the sisters with you, which means there will now be 32 of you,4 and in early February I shall send more. Goodbye. I have received all your letters. Goodbye, your

affectionate M.Rosa

1 Sr. A. Ermanna Cerri, Sr. A. Mansueta Campitelli and Sr. A. Fedele Zanni.

2 The two Sisters, as she says below, are Sr. A. Felicita Maggioli and Sr. A. Berarda Cattani.

3 The two sisters needed proper religious formation, which is why she had entrusted them to her.

4 The Genoa nursing community was large so as to meet the many requests for home nursing of the sick.

Thanks and expressions of affection.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

  1. How can one remain unmoved by so many signs of affection? Oh! I shall always say it: love is ingenious, love knows how to find a way to show its affection!!2

  2. Endless thanks for the wine you sent. God reward you; pray for me and believe me yours in my dear Crucified One.

affectionate M.Rosa

1 The date is deduced from the context, especially from a letter of Sr. A. Irene dated 17.1.1878.

2 Among other things she wrote that she would send the fruit and try to get other things to bring her in person.

She replies to the notice that the FSA's engagement in the Tor de' Specchi school has ended and declares herself ready to help in other charitable activities.

[Most Illustrious Ladies,]1

1. I am deeply touched by the expressions Your Ladyships have been pleased to send me, though the praise you give the poor Daughters of Saint Anne is undeserved, since they did nothing to merit thanks, I being bound to repay the many favours received from the most noble Princess Altieri, to whom I declare myself ever ready,2 whenever I can serve her, to show my eternal gratitude, and [I shall do so] most willingly.

  1. Let the St Monica Circle count on the Daughters of Saint Anne, who will always be ready to offer their humble service whenever it considers them needed.

  2. Returning my warmest thanks, I have the honour to sign myself, with the highest esteem, Your Most Illustrious Ladyships'

Humble Devoted Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 To understand the reason for this letter one must explain what had happened at the Tor de' Specchi school, mentioned in Lettere 4, L 393; L 406, nn. 6-9.

The church authorities had asked the Oblates of Tor de' Specchi to house in their monastery a community of enclosed nuns who had no home, and had received a favourable reply: they could give up the premises previously lent to the ladies of the St Monica Circle for the school and the attached lodging of the teaching Sisters, Daughters of Saint Anne. The ladies, so as not to close

the school, made do by fitting it into just two rooms; the Sisters were left without lodging, nor could any rooms be found for them nearby. For her part, Mother Rosa did not think it right for them to live in the Vicolo Margana house. At this point the ladies entrusted the school to other teachers. They informed the Mother of these events, thanking her and praising her excellent daughters for their work for the benefit of the poor girls of Rome. The letter was written on their behalf by the President, Maria Schneider.

2 Princess Bice Altieri, formerly President of the St Monica Circle and deeply attached to M.Rosa, had helped her in her good works; she keeps a fond memory of them and is ever ready to serve her as a sign of gratitude.

She deals with the transfer of some Sisters to and from Sestri Ponente. She asks her to visit the Albaro house and do what is best.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have received yours and hear that you obeyed at once;1 now the Superior Sr. A. Innocenza begs me to give her back the sister who was so good for the schools. Listen, let us try again and see; you can send her,2 and then you can take back Sr. A. Mansueta, unless you want to leave her there in place of Sr. A. Berarda; see what you think.3

  2. The superior says she needs a cook and a capable sister as teacher; that is what she wanted; it is enough to give her back Sr. A. Felicita.

  3. Now I enclose a letter for the Superior at Albaro, for I hear from others that they are truly pitiful, so poor are they.4 Listen, write me something and tell her that I absolutely do not want Sr. A. Fausta ever to go nursing the sick.5 Write me something. Goodbye,

your affectionate M.Rosa

1 She had gone to Sestri to fetch Sr. A. Felicita, as the Mother had told her. Cf. L 11,2.

2 The Superior at Sestri had, however, asked her to assign Sr. A. Felicita to her community, as she seemed capable and suited to the school.

3 ...you can take back ...Berarda. She could also take back Sr. A. Mansueta, the other Sister sent to Sestri, but left her free to decide whether to leave her there in place of Sr. A. Berarda.

4 She had learned that the Sisters were living in great poverty. Cf. L 6.

5 Sr. A. Fausta Torriani was the teacher of the little school.

She asks him to grant a dowry to a poor young woman admitted to the Institute.

[Your Excellency,]

  1. The undersigned begs the charity of Your Most Illustrious Excellency to admit to the distribution of dowries intended for poor young women who wish to become religious.1

  2. Of these, N.N., an orphan lacking everything, even the barest necessities, has already been admitted to our poor Institute, and that is why we turn to Your Excellency, asking you to consider her and send her one of the dowries Your Excellency distributes in cases of such need.2 Trusting to obtain everything from your kindness, I profess myself Your Excellency's

Most humble Servant [Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno]

1 She asks that poor young women wishing to enter the Institute be counted among the possible beneficiaries.

2 He should consider the young orphan who has already entered.

Advice about a Sister who, for health reasons, should return home for a time, needing her native air.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. A line because you tell me about the Sister. Be patient; try to urge her to write to her relatives to come and fetch her, or else send her to me for a change of air, for she could surely recover.2 So with your kind ways you will be able to persuade her, won't you?

  2. So do all you can; besides, this way you will be more at peace and not have so many worries over the sick.

Goodbye; courage, for we shall soon see each other.

Your affectionate M.Rosa

1 The date is deduced from Sr. A. Guglielma's reply.

2 On 26 January the superior replied that she had informed the father of Sr. A. Tedalda De Paoli.

She explains how to deal with the postulants. She will take them to Naples after giving notice. She has asked the Mayor to pay the salaries.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received all the letters, and also one from the Canon commending the two postulants to me. I replied that I accept them and that they should get ready; so they will come with you to Naples.

  1. Mind that they must each have 500 F. Do you understand? And that besides the journey; you can gather them all, the others too, and if you could persuade the Mayor's daughter,1 for it really [is] a pity she stays as she is. See if there are others, and so you will gather a good harvest.

  2. I have spoken about the salary,2 both for you and for the infant-school Sister, and I would really like you to insist, so that you can collect it before coming, which will be in mid or late February.

4. I shall write well beforehand; indeed, if there is [a] telegraph, I would let you know two days before, telling you the exact day I shall leave. What do you say? Write and tell me if there is one.3 Many greetings to the Superior and the sisters. Believe me your affectionate M.Rosa

1 Persuade the Mayor's daughter. Persuade the Mayor's daughter to leave, as she had long expressed the wish to enter the Institute.

2 I have spoken to him ... She had written to him urging payment of the Sisters, since the monthly payments were not on time.

3 The Sister replies that there is.

She assures her that she will look after her mother and father. She awaits news of the new house she is about to go to.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter,

  1. I hope you received mine in Florence; now I see1 yours written from Florence and I bless God for having given Mamma peace and patience.2

  2. Be sure I shall not fail to think of Mamma; as you will know, I have also given Papa something; what can I do, it is so hard to find a suitable place for Mamma that I really don't know where to turn, but in any case I keep her always in mind and shall never forget to recommend her.3

  3. Meanwhile I want you to write me something from there about the schools and whether you are happy there; we shall soon see each other.4

  4. Yes, my dear daughter; love your spouse greatly and place everything in Him; you will see that you will have what you desire. Be joyful in Jesus, where I leave you, and remain for ever your

affectionate M.Rosa Gattorno

1 She had just begun the letter when she received hers, from Florence.

2 Her mother had resigned herself to her daughter's departure from Florence.

3 Sr. A. Letizia commends her mother to her; she has a small child and needs lodgings, which the father, being poor, cannot provide.

4 She wants her to write from Appignano, where she is about to go.

Advice on how to deal with the Mayor and the school Inspector about the salary.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear the Mayor will not let you draw water; why? is he angry? whatever has happened? try to find out the reason.1 My opinion would be not to mention this to the Inspector, but rather to find the cause and then put it right.2

2. Just write to him or else go3 to the Inspector and tell him your salary is small and you cannot live on it, and what you lack, and then say nothing more; I would only add whether we might have more so as to hire a woman to draw water for us,4 because one has to go to the square and we cannot, it is so deep, and besides we cannot go to the square.5 Your affectionate M.Rosa

1 As there was no running water in the town, the Sisters drew water from the we-ll in the neighbouring courtyard, which belonged to the Mayor. But, as the Superior writes, he had forbidden them to use it.

2 The Superior had proposed her own solution: to speak to the Inspector about it.

3 Here is the precise advice: you must put your general financial situation, caused by the unfair salary, to the Inspector in person.

4 As for the well, a secondary problem, she advises only a pass-ing mention of the suitable remedy: hiring a woman.

5 The Mayor later explained to the Superior the reason for his refusal: there is little water and he is not obliged to pay for it for us. Cf. L of C. Cenni to M.Rosa of 4.2.78.

She sends her a parish priest's letter of recommendation. She asks for news.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste to send you the letter I forgot to give you when I came to Pistoia.2 You will see it is a letter of recommendation given me by a Parish Priest who does so much good for us, and I assure you that by presenting it you will benefit.3 I shall send the candlesticks.

Goodbye, your most affectionate [M.R.]

2. Tell me, has Sr. A. Clelia's cousin come?4 Did he bring the money? For pity's sake. You know, as for the portrait, taken to Florence never, to Pistoia never.5 Goodbye, your affectionate M.Rosa

So in Florence you can also make out the money order to send it to me when he brings it.

1 The date is deduced from the correspondent's reply to the questions in par. 2 below.

2 She had gone to Pistoia on 4 January. Cf. L 3; 4; 5.

3 A letter with excellent references, to be shown to people who do not know the Institute.

4 Sr. A. Clelia Semeria.

5 The said Sister's relatives wanted a photograph of her.

She urges her to live intensely the Lord's presence in her heart and to work and love for Him and in Him alone.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. If only we all worked our own little patch of ground that God has given us to cultivate, and made in ours a solitary dwelling, and thought of nothing but loving and serving the good God, and in the solitude of this inner room set up an altar to adore our dear Jesus alone!1 [then] indeed nothing else could come to wound our ears, but we would always be intent on listening to his voice, which can be heard only in the room of solitude!

  2. Blessed are you who can withdraw from work into the room of retreat! So, suffer, suffer and love.2 Ears closed, heart open, and work and love in Him alone, for Him alone.3 But!

  3. Mercatello is a cruel thorn piercing my soul, because I know God is offended there.4 Alas! Alas! Have pity on Jesus! (and) I am

your affectionate and deeply grieved Mother

1 The Sister had written that in this new house (at Mercatello) she felt as if in prison and missed the happy days in the Piacenza community. The Mother directs her along the uphill path of following Christ: to live for Him alone, adoring Him in the depths of the heart and listening to Him. Alone with the Alone.

2 Work and prayer, an inseparable pair, alongside another equally fundamental one: suffering and loving.

3 Ears closed to all that can wound us and heart open to love, to give ourselves to Him without reserve, and to work and love in Him.

4 Charity was lacking in the community; Sr. A. Maddalena felt hurt by the way some Sisters treated her.

She has received her little letter. She rejoices at her fine dispositions of love for the Work of God and offers her to Jesus.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your very dear little letter1 saying that you want everything for your dear Institute and your whole life for it. My daughter! mine! blessed one! You love your Institute and a thousand sacrifices for It.2 Oh! Jesus! Hold my dear Sr. A. Letizia close for me and consume her in your love!3 Yes, the work of God! And what's more, write to me often, tell me many lovely things, and we shall soon see each other. Yours for ever

affectionate M.Rosa

1 The letter is dated 29 January '78.

2 She wrote, in these words, assuring her that she would "be faithful to her and work hard for the glory of the Institute".

3 With a mother's surge of love the Mother entrusts to Jesus her dear Letizia, so young (she is 19), at the beginning of religious life, and tried in her family by poverty and misfortune. Cf. L 18.

Having heard of Canon Biagini's illness, she sends him a blessing from the Holy Father.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line to tell you that the news of the Canon's illness1 has grieved me very much, and at once I thought of having him blessed by the Holy Father, who blesses him2 with all his heart. Tell him at once, and tell him that we are praying and having prayers said, and that if he were a little nearer I would fly there to show him my eternal gratitude myself.3 Meanwhile I add nothing, as I want this to reach you at once.

2. Give me news every day, for pity's sake, for I am in the greatest anxiety. Goodbye; give him my warmest greetings, and tell him how sorry I am.

Goodbye.

Your affectionate M.Rosa

1 The Superior Giuseppa had written to her on 1 February that Canon Angelo Biagini was ill and she had sat up with him.

2 dove la benedire: who blesses him.

3 The Canon was a benefactor of the Institute. Cf. L 9, n. 4.

Worried about her health, she urges her to take care of herself. She should write to her father, enclosing the letter with hers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Just a line: I have received your letters and hear that your health is not too good. My God! What happened? Take care of yourself and get well soon; I await this anxiously. •

  2. I am delighted to know you are happy. Listen, write two lines to your father and put them in mine; as soon as he comes I shall give them to him.2 Write them at once.

  3. Your words are a real comfort to me. God strengthen you in his love, dear daughter. Yes, we shall soon see each other3.

  4. I am so swamped with a thousand affairs that they force me to close, declaring myself yours for all ages

affectionate M.Rosa

1 The Sister, unused to the cold climate, had caught a bad cough with chest pain.

2 As soon as the letter arrives she will pass it on to her.

3 Yes, we shall see each other soon. This was Sr. A. Letizia's greatest wish.

An invitation to come to Rome with the postulants.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste. Come at once and bring the postulants with you to Rome, so we can spend a little time together and then I shall take you to Naples.1 Are you pleased? Come with the postulants.

Goodbye, I shall soon embrace you.

Your affectionate M.Rosa

1 The Mother had told her earlier that she would let her know when to come and accompany the postulants. Cf. L 17.

She rejoices at the good start of the boarding school. She asks prayers for the election of the new Pope and the Cardinal Protector's health. Advice.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. At last the time has come to write two lines in reply to your long letters, which I was never, never able to do, being extremely busy; goodbye1, a little relieved, and at once my thoughts run to my dear Giuseppina, to show her that I read her letters and that they are very dear to me and give me pleasure, especially when I hear that this little boarding school is beginning to flourish, or at least is taking a good turn.2 Blessed be God for it, who helps his poor Daughters of Saint Anne so well and with such mercy.

  1. Pray and have prayers said for the election of the new Pope,3 that he may be wholly for the Daughters of Saint Anne, and pray also for our Protector, that he may recover, for he is not too well.4

  2. And do our girls still have their uniform? Try to do all you can so that it can be obtained, even if they paid a little at a time; we could get it and then have them pay so much a month;5 what do you say? Be of good heart, for when we go to Piacenza and the cold is over you will come with us. Meanwhile organize the boarding school well so that it can run without you.6

Goodbye.

Your affectionate M.Rosa

1 ... busy... goodbye. The meaning is unclear. Perhaps she meant to wri-te: today, thank God, I am a little relieved...

2 The boarding school in Florence is getting under way thanks to Sr. A. Giuseppina's skill.

3 Pius IX had died on 7.2.1878. On 20.2.78 Leo XIII was elected. He had already met Mother Rosa.

4 Cardinal Giuseppe Berardi.

5 She suggests advancing the cost and making the uniforms. Each boarder would then pay for her own, perhaps in monthly instalments.

6 Can run: can go on well without your presence.

She should accept the postulant. She should advise Canon Biagini to draw up a deed in favour of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear you did not receive mine in which I told you that I accept the postulant you proposed and that you should send her to Piacenza at once.

  2. Listen, try tactfully to tell the Canon to give me the consolation of drawing up a proper deed,1 leaving whatever he wishes to the Daughters of Saint Anne, for we shall certainly give God great pleasure, and then there could be no further danger.2 For pity's sake, let him do so.

  3. Tell him I have sent a fine picture of Saint Anne. I hope you will receive [it] together with this. Tell the Canon that he should give me this consolation of doing everything as I say above. The Cardinal too would be very pleased, and sends him [his blessing].3

  4. When you are sure that the two sisters are alone with the lady, then they can sleep there, as you say.4

Goodbye, I am in haste, your affectionate M.R.

1 Canon Angelo Biagini had not made a will; he had only made over a flat in his house by means of a nominal lease. Now the Mother wanted him to draw up a precise notarial deed.

2 No danger: because his relatives were doing all they could to get the house for themselves.

3 The Cardinal Protector Giuseppe Berardi.

4 A lady living alone in the same palazzo, on the floor below, asked for two Sisters to sleep at her home when she felt ill. Cf. L of G. Troni 21.2.78 to M.Rosa.

She will have the school syllabus sent to her. Advice and recommendations about her health.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear you want the syllabus; I am writing at once to Onorata1 to send it to you. Now listen, I want to hear that you are completely well, and I don't want you ill at all;2 in short, don't strain your voice, let the others do it; until you are well, don't tire yourself, do you understand? This is what I ardently wish. When I come I hope to find you really well.

2. Your dear and affectionate words are a real balm to me, and God knows how great my affection is for my dear daughter. So, courage; I must close. Give the superior my best, and believe me for all ages your affectionate M. Sr. A. Rosa

1 Onorata Colli.

2 Cf. L 24.

She explains the meaning of the notarial deed to be suggested to Canon Biagini. Advice about her going to Nizza and accepting the postulants.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. This is what I meant by the word deed.1 You know, a contract like the one I had shown him, which would be like a life annuity; it appears as if he had made the annuity with us,2 and he already knows how. I sent him the form; the Canon knows about it. Oh! how glad I would be if he did it! He would spare himself so much trouble and have no more bother; so see if you can obtain what I write; I assure you I would be really happy. Oh yes, the Canon ought to give me this consolation.

  2. Now to you and your going to Nizza. Listen, if you could at least put it off until early April, then we could think about it, but now I am afraid to send a new one.3 See what you can do.

  3. As for the older postulant, you see about it; before accepting her observe her well and find out everything;4 as for the other, who has 500 F., get them from her and keep them for me until I write and tell you where to send them.

  4. If the postulant could be ready in Florence by Monday, she could leave with the others. See that she has the travel money.

  5. As for the cloth, it is better for you to get it ready for me,5 and when I come you will give [it] to me and I shall pay for it all together with what I have had sent here.

Goodbye; many greetings to the Canon, give him my best, and also to his servant and [his] sister, and believe me your affectionate M. Sr. A. Rosa

2 A contract "vita naturale durante" (for life).

4 The postulant, introduced by a priest, was 40.

Congratulations on her recovery. She awaits her in Rome.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Your letter was a real consolation to me;2 you surely cannot imagine it. God bless you; the Heart of Jesus rejoices in his daughter.

  2. See you soon; (your) I shall tell you many things in person. Courage, and care3 for your health, so that you can always work for the glory of God and the good of poor humanity, that it may not be lost.

Goodbye, the Lord bless you, and believe me ever your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The date is deduced from the Sister's L.

2 She had given her excellent news: she had recovered and resumed teaching.

3 Courage, and take care of your health so that you can always work...

Advice and encouragement.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Just a line to tell you it is good that you write to your uncle, but say nothing to him about the sisters;1 only assure him that you will go and visit him in July.

  2. For the rest all is well, and I tell you to be of good heart and always cheerful and content.2

  3. How glad your letter made me, with such good news of your house. I wish you a thousand blessings from Heaven, and may God make you grow in His Holy love.

Your affectionate M. Rosa

1 She answers the L of 28.2.78 in which the Sister said she was sorry to learn that her uncle had refused to receive her fellow Sisters (perhaps those col-lecting alms); she put this down perhaps to the newly hired maid. She ask-ed whether she should tell her uncle.

She asks him to keep an eye on the work in progress at the Piacenza house: the wall at the end of the garden and the building of a wing added to the novitiate.

Most devoted Count,

1. A line in haste before leaving for Naples, where I shall stay 8 days. For your guidance, address letters to Gaspare, who will reply for me; we are all anxious for the good news that the preliminary agreement has been made and the property is at our disposal.1

2. I had told my master builder, the Venetian, to make a manger for the cow,2 but if we are lucky enough to buy the garden it would no longer be needed; what do you think? If so, would you kindly let him know.

  1. I would also ask a further, greater kindness, on top of the many countless ones I always receive: to keep an eye on the wall they are to start building at the end of the garden and on the small wing they are adding to the novitiate.3

  2. It pains me to think that I am far away and can only direct things by letter; he gave me an estimate of about ¥.400; I already have much of the material.

  3. You will receive some money from Ventimiglia; please do with it as you did with the rest and put it together in the bank. What a lot of trouble! The cause [of] it all is having a tiresome, bothersome Friend full of wretchedness.

Greetings to all; I really must close. I am your affectionate Friend Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 Gaspare... disposal. Gaspare Barbiellini would reply, as he too was directly involved in drawing up the preliminary agreement to buy part of the garden and adjoining buildings (dwelling house, farm buildings, gardener's cottage) next to the motherhouse.

2 The master builder Gaetano Rovelli, known as the Venetian.

3 The master builder had already begun the work. AFSA Motherhouse Documents, Piacenza.

She explains how to deal with a Sister in connection with a letter sent to her. She should then go to Sestri to visit the community. Recommendations.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Now I want a favour, but in complete secrecy, so that nobody knows anything of what I write; so what you have to do, you must do in silence, I beg you. Listen, [as for] (if) my letter written for Sr. A. Consolata,2 do this: if she has come and read it, say nothing more;3 but if she has not read it because she had already left, then open the letter and go to Sestri without telling anyone, and do yourself what Sr. A. Consolata was to do, but prudently and in silence; put your own name.4

  1. Listen, I forgot to send her this letter;5 if she is there, give it to her; if not, do this: read it yourself and see what those poor sisters say; but you must never tackle things head on, but calmly and gently do everything so that the unfortunate woman does not fly into a rage.6

  2. Please see to it; for your guidance, I shall be in Naples until Saturday or Monday the 16th inst., if you need to write to me.

  3. I commend Sr. A. Felicita to you; I think of her constantly. I am very glad you have decided to keep Sr. A. Giusta!7 God reward you for the good you do, while I wish you a thousand blessings from Heaven, and am

your affectionate M. Sr. A. Rosa

Have prayers said, for I am not too well. Goodbye.

1 The date is deduced from the addressee's replies.

2 Sr. A. Consolata Massimelli.

3 Sr. A. Amabile replied to the Mother that on 13 March Sr. A. Consolata was present when her letter arrived and she handed it to her at once.

4 Put your own name. She means: if the Sister had left, you would wri-te your name on the envelope, to show that the Mother had given her that task with the Sestri community.

5 She had meant to send the letter directly to the person concerned but forgot, so she encloses it with hers.

6 the unfortunate woman does not fly into a rage: that the poor Sister, who is not behaving well, does not get angry.

7 Sr. A. Felicita: cf. L 14, n. 1. Sr. A. Giusta: on this Sr. A. Amabile had written "I keep her with me and have her treated my way." Cf. L of 13.3.78 to M. Rosa.

She encourages her to get well and come to Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear you are better. Oh! Dear Jesus! So courage, get up soon, come to Rome, I am waiting for you.1 Mary and Saint Anne want you well, no more cough, no more.2 I am in haste; write and tell me you are well and I shall tell you who you are to come with. Goodbye.

Your affectionate M. Sr. A. Rosa

1 An urgent invitation to trust. Jesus has heard her prayer. So she must get up; she awaits her in Rome.

2 Healthy people are needed in the Lord's Work.

She asks her to choose a capable and suitable Sister for the Bordighera community and send her off.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Now I come for a big favour. Listen, dear daughter, I need a good, sensible sister, without a tongue1 and, you understand me, strong and a good nurse, for Bordighera; so send her there at once.

  2. I leave the choice to you, but let it be as I say. For pity's sake, at once, for the need is extreme. On Saturday I shall be back in Rome.2 Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa G.

1 Without a tongue: she means quiet and discreet.

2 Saturday 16 March.

Advice about a postulant and her going to Nizza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear what you say about the postulant; you can do this: as for the savings book, she must cash it and give you the money.1

  2. The rest do this way: since the Canon is well and you tell me everything is in order, you should pop over to Nizza, pay the bills and collect the payment orders. See whether I can have something.2

  3. Give the postulant's money to Sr. A. Nazzarena in a sealed envelope. She will put it where she knows, with the rest, in our room. That is what I think best.

  4. Now as for the furniture, you are right, she can leave it all to you.3 Leaving together, she will be company for you.

  5. This evening at 9 I shall be back in Rome, God willing. For pity's sake, try to leave everything in order and return soon to Pistoia. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Sr. A. Rosa

She charges her with sending home a Sister who wants to leave the Institute.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear that this sister, to whom you will give this letter, wants to go home.

  2. Listen, it is not good for you to take them head on like that.1 Enough; send her to Piacenza at once.

  3. I am very sorry you sent Sr. A. Felice to Bordighera. Ah! she was not a suitable sister! Patience!2

4. Treat this sister gently and see that everything is quite secure.3 Goodbye, I am in haste, your affectionate M. Rosa

She remembers her. Recommendations about her health. She will give her an assistant for the school.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I received your letter, and now, although I cannot write to you in my own hand,1 rest assured that I always have you near me. Try to keep well and take your examinations soon, so that you can come to Piacenza to rest.2

  2. Meanwhile I am writing to the Superior to give you Sr. A. Pelagia to help you in school (so you will be less burdened). For now I am not moving,3 but soon I hope to set sail for Piacenza. It will be next month. Sr. A. Benedetta thanks you for the work you did for us; she has received everything.4

Greet the sisters for me. The Lord bless you most affectionate M. Rosa

P.S. Be cheerful, for you will be content. Yours for ever, your affectionate M. RosaS

2. Listen, the shawl has not arrived yet, but we need the receipt and to know how it was sent,2 by steamer or by post. Please write and tell me.

3. How is your melancholy? I want you to write me lots of things. Goodbye, yours for ever affectionate M. Sr. A. Rosa

Instructions about handing over the money and about the Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear you cannot leave until Wednesday,1 and that Sr. A. Clelia's money has reached you.2 Thanks be to God; take it, together with the postulant's, to Sr. A. Nazzarena3 and tell her for pity's sake to put it where it cannot be stolen or lost, for pity's sake. For the rest, all you tell me is fine.

And so we are sure we shall rejoin our loved ones! And is it not a great comfort for you to know that your Father is in a place of salvation?

She asks him to oversee personally the drawing up of the deeds of sale for the properties.

My dear Count,

  1. Here I am back in Rome,1 where I saw papers and letters from that wretched Cipelli.2 It seems to me a curious and very tangled affair. How will it turn out? Carla is impatient; on the other hand, what she wants cannot be granted.3

  2. I commend the matter to you as earnestly as I can; for pity's sake let everything be done clearly and in proper order, because he is such a quibbler4 that in the end we shall have nothing but serious trouble. What do you think? As long as you see to it, all will go well, for with your shrewdness and wisdom it cannot go otherwise.

  3. You will receive R4000 through the National Bank; please deposit it in the same bank as you did with the rest, since I do not want to carry it with me on the journey, having several houses to visit.

  1. So it is always new trouble and bother! Oh! my dear Count, only your goodness could put up with such a nuisance.

  2. Have you seen the work? Is the wall coming up high? I would like it to be really high, so that we cannot be seen from the Passeggio, which is necessary for a large community of women.5

  3. Have you bought the wheat? And for the cow, have you seen whether there is a suitable place? If so, the mason can make the manger at once.6

  4. This letter brings a world of bother. That is what comes of being charitable. Many greetings to all, and receive a million thanks and affectionate7 tokens from one who signs herself

Your affectionate Friend Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She will send the image of Our Lady and what they asked for as soon as possible.

Dearest daughters,

1. I am answering you both;2 I am sending you the pictures; for the Madonna I went at once but could not find one; there will be one in 10 days; I had it ordered at once and shall send it straight away; it will cost £.8.

  1. Very well; as for the little doll's, I have not been able to get it yet; as soon as it is returned to me I shall send it;3 likewise I am waiting for the Saint's coat of arms from Piacenza.4

  2. Be patient, dear daughters; if you knew how much work I found! Enough. Goodbye. Warm greetings to Sr. Orsolina,5 and to the Priests too, and I am yours in my Dear Crucified One

affectionate M. Rosa

She rebukes her for her behaviour towards a Sister and instructs her on the need for correction by Superiors and on relations with them.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I read yours in bed,1 but I was scandalized to hear that you call a sister a vassal for having written to me.2 And even if she had spoken ill to me, should you be upset? Oh! this is really too much, to be upset that our superiors3 know our faults!

  1. This is real pride and the subtlest arrogance; you should be glad that the mother knows everything!

  2. What? Should we not be corrected by our Superiors? Who loves us more than our Superiors? Oh! daughter! ask Jesus to make you one heart with your Superiors; otherwise you will never run well and will always fall into error!4

  3. Have you understood? So, courage and frankness with Superiors. Goodbye; I urge you to observance and to be very careful about the reports.5 Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

3 Our Superiors: herself and Fr Tornatore.

  1. I hear from yours that you did not receive my letter. Never mind; I have the censer and hope to send it to you soon; I also have another postulant here whom I shall send, and you will send them off together.1

  2. You could have asked more for the girls so as not to lose out.2 Never mind; you will hear in person, God willing.

  1. Meanwhile send Sr. A. Amalia to Gualdo Tadino, for the Superior is expecting her.3

  1. I would not want you to repeat these things; take care not to let them slip out.

  2. How is Uppello going? I would like the boys too to go to school, so that they also would become good.7

My daughter,

  1. I hear the good news you give me of the sisters and am truly happy.1 I would not go; or else, if you think it right to go, you two go to Arona and see.2

  2. Tell the sisters that I am not writing to them because I am weighed down with work, but that I hold them to my heart in the heart of Jesus, urging them to love and serve Him.3

your affectionate M. Rosa

The Cipelli affair is not settled. She asks him to see to it and hurry it along.

  1. The Daughters of Saint Anne would be ready to satisfy this just desire if they had premises large enough to take in the many children who would come; and so, there being no more suitable place, I turn to you to ask that you kindly grant me in charity a part of the Convent where the Friars Minor Observant live,4 the part the friars do not occupy and do not need, promising that they will not be inconvenienced in any way.

  2. With this work, truly worthy of all praise, you would add, Most Illustrious Marchioness, another great merit to the many you already have before God; and not only will the blessings of the poor little ones who through your generosity find a place where they can learn to grow up good and religious, lovers of truth and of work, descend abundantly upon your head, but the humble prayers of the poor Daughters of Saint Anne will also rise to God for your welfare.

5. In the hope of obtaining what I humbly ask, full of veneration I present my respectful greetings and declare myself Your Ladyship's

Most devoted Servant Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno

1 The date is deduced from the correspondence of Sr. A. Coletta Faccini, of the community at the house of Mrs Maddalena Parmigiani. Cf. CsIS, D9.

2 Every Sunday after Mass Sr. A. Coletta used to gather the "wayward girls" in order to make them "Children of Mary". The Parish Priest, Fr Domenico Costa, approved of the initiative but had no room to offer. So the meet-ings were held in the courtyard of a house just outside the town, which the lady owner had offered, trusting the Sister. Cf. L 18.4.1878 to M. Rosa.

3 The Mother, realizing the need, wanted to gather the boys too and instruct them in Christian doctrine.

4 The Friars Minor Observant served the church of the Santissima Annunziata, given to them with the adjoining convent by Count Ludovico Pallavicino (founder of Cortemaggiore) in the 16th century. The Marchioness therefore had great influence with them.

Spiritual exhortations on the love of God and its fruits in time and eternity.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your dear little letter was a real consolation to me; you speak of sacrifices and I see they are hard for you to bear.1 Daughter! What is there more beautiful, more dear (than) for one who loves that object, who alone is worthy of our love, and to possess his? Oh! Daughter, what does it take? Sacrifices, crosses, pains, suffering!!!2 and fighting as true soldiers of the eternal homeland of Heaven, where who reigns? who? the most beautiful, the sweetest of all beings that dwell on earth or in heaven.3

  1. Love is his name,4 and only those who knew how to fight well and win, whose breasts are covered with medals of honour, yes, only to these has he given a taste of the purest balm of this Love.

  2. Oh! may you be consumed, may it burn you to ashes!5 Love, love, and then do what you will, says St Augustine. Yes, whoever loves cannot displease the beloved, so that in all they do they keep that sweet fear of erring and displeasing.6 Holy fear, sweet and dear, you are nothing but a band that binds the heart of love!7

I would never stop, and yet I must finish because time is short. Your affectionate, more than all the world, your M. Rosa

1 The Sister had written to her: "since you, my Mother, are no longer here, Rome is a desert for me. Our poor Cardinal (Berardi) is gone, you left us. Our Superior Santina remained, and she too... the Lord took her from us as well... the Lord has wanted great sacrifices from us." The Mother starts from this existential situation of discouragement and opens it to the understanding of a transcendent reality.

2 There is only one object worthy of our love, and to possess it one must face sacrifices, crosses, pains, suffering. Cf. Mt 7:14; 11:12.

3 the most beautiful, the sweetest, titles recalling Ps 45 (44): "you are the fairest of the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips."

4 Love is his name. 1 Jn 4:7 "God is love."

5 burn you to ashes. A wish born of lofty mystical experience, such as she herself had known.

6 Pure love cannot be separated from the fear of displeasing the beloved.

7 Cf. 2 Cor 7:11; Col 3:22; Heb 12:28-29.

She hopes to go to Appignano. Affectionate encouragement.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Just a line to tell you that yours gave me much pleasure; so, God willing, I really hope to come and bring the superior myself.1

  2. You did well about the money for your mother;2 always do so, that is right; and courage, away with melancholy, always be cheerful and you will see that the Lord will bless you. I would like to tell you many things, but I have so much to do and it is late.3 Goodbye, your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Superior had had to leave the community for health reasons.

2 Sr. A. Pacifica Bassi, who was standing in for the Superior, sent a small allowance to her mother every month, noting the sum in a separate little notebook. Cf. letters L Sordi to M. Rosa.

3 ... and it is late. The Mother often wrote to her daughters into the small hours.

She has received the order to withdraw the Sisters gradually from the Florence house and close it. She expresses deep sorrow and amazement, unable to understand the reasons. She sets out the good being done there. She is ready to go to Florence with his permission.

Your Excellency,

  1. I have just finished reading your esteemed letter and reply by return of post.2 My God! The wound it gave me is such3 that I do not know how I shall put these two lines together, so I beg your pardon first of all for the effort you will have to make to understand what I am about to say.

  2. Most Reverend Excellency, however much I ponder the reason for such terrible news, I cannot come to understand it; if it were the incident of the Sister who left, had it been told to Your Most Reverend Excellency truthfully, that would certainly not be the reason.4

  3. So, passing through Florence, I found it was good to change the Superior5 and I did so; but one voice, indeed more than one, I heard saying: "take away the Superior and the House will blow up too. Oh! We shall see to it that it happens"; I chose to pay no attention to this; I went to your Vicar and also to the Canon, whom I did not find.

  4. The Vicar assured me that there was nothing, that I had done well to change the Superior, and that what had happened (his very words) was childishness.6

5. The incident of the Sister:7 finding herself placed under strict discipline by the new Superior, she began to complain; and what did she do? She went out alone to the Confessor... she was sure of support. He took her to Ciaranfi, and the Superior, informed, went to fetch her and took her away... setting off at once for Piacenza. If this is a misdeed so ugly that it can bring us infamy, I believe!!!

  1. And Your Most Reverend Excellency is too wise not to weigh what several spiteful and slanderous people can do,8 just as, while I was in Florence, people were reading of two incidents involving the Sisters of Charity and two little girls, for which they even had to appear before the Magistrate, and nothing was done to them; I arrived here and another Sister of Charity had run off with a young man, and nothing;9 and I report the matters of those Sisters.

  2. Most Reverend Excellency, ah! have pity on this your poorest servant, to whom you were always so kind,10 and who was in all things frank and obedient to you. Why punish me so harshly? Without coming to a summons?11

  3. Listen, Most Reverend Excellency, I shall go at once to Florence and stay there a good while, and I shall keep Your Most Reverend Excellency informed of everything; and you will advise me on whatever displeases you, and I shall try to remove it.12

  4. A house that did and does so much good! The schools were visited by the Inspector, who was pleased, so much so that the Municipality granted them a salary, and they are really doing well; the boarders are numerous, and so are the sick. I have very fine letters of thanks; I do not have them here, but I read them in Florence; there are so many requests that I had to send two more sisters; Providence is very generous.

  1. Excellency, ah! for pity's sake, appoint a Priest to give the Holy Exercises; then you can be informed of the truth about the good spirit. I cannot think of so sad a thing without feeling my soul torn apart; and if in the past you were pleased with the House, you will be so again.

  2. Believe me, a great deal of good is done. Not long ago they obtained that an unhappy man, after many years of bad living, who would have nothing to do with priests or God, died in the arms of Holy Religion. How well the little girls are taught the Catechism! If you saw them you would be pleased.

12. Oh! no! I will not think of this sad news. It grieves me too much!13 I trust in the fatherly clemency you have always shown me; meanwhile, as I inform the Protector whom the Holy Father in his goodness gave to the Institute, approved as it is by Holy Church, I must report everything and await obedience; so before leaving here I await a line from you to reassure me and tell me that I shall always be a small portion of your flock. Meanwhile, wretched as I am, I shall not cease to pray the good God to grant you all the graces Your Most Reverend Excellency desires.

  1. Excellency, you surely know that the Institute has 52 houses, and I can assure you in all truth that I have never had the slightest complaint from the Diocesans;14 and in all the Dioceses they are not content with one house or two; I am obliged to refuse requests. Make enquiries about the Houses of Naples, Pistoia, etc.

  2. Excellency, one line, for pity's sake, for I cannot bear to think!! Oh! your charity grants me everything; I seem already to have what I desire: your pardon with your Holy Pastoral Blessing, while, prostrate at your feet full of veneration, I remain Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most humble and devoted Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

PS. As soon as I have your letter I shall leave at once.

1 The date is deduced from the Archbishop's letter written from Rome on 4.5.1878. AFSA.CvIC, F69.

2 The Mother replies by return of post.

3 The wound is such. The Archbishop writes that he has learned "recently from Florence that the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, as presently constituted, cannot produce in my Diocese the good that it seemed to at first" and therefore invites her "to make arrangements... so that gradually and without publicity the Florence House may be dissolved as soon as possible."

4 However much I ponder... reason. The Mother cannot find the reason for such terrible news; she supposes it is the incident of the Sister who left the Institute, but does not think this can be the reason for such a measure.

5 Passing through Florence, on the way back from Rome, she had thought it right to change the Superior, Sr. A. Del Salvatore Orsi. Sr. A. Santina Solenghi had replaced her.

6 She had made the change despite dissenting voices, had informed his Vicar General and received his full approval; she had also called on Canon Luigi Ciaranfi, Vicar for Nuns, but had not found him.

7 The incident of the Sister mentioned above: paragraph 2, n. 4.

8 what... can do: what various spiteful and slanderous people can or usually do.

9 She reports two serious incidents involving other Sisters, one in Florence, the other in Piacenza, for which no houses were closed.

10 to whom you were always so kind, towards whom you were always kind.

11 Without going as far as an order to meet for a necessary clarification.

12 I shall try to remove it, to change whatever you wish.

13 Sad news, that is, the closure of the house.

14 from the Diocesans: from the Bishops of the various dioceses.

For a Sister who is unhappy and has family problems, she advises sending her to her in Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. A hasty line to tell you to tell the Sister to be at peace, for everything will be sorted out.1 It would be good for you to send her for a while to S. Martinello, and tell the superior to take her mind off things a little.

  2. I fear, though, that there may be something more, and then it would be good for you to send her straight here at once.2 I think it better not to have her stop anywhere, on the pretext that she is coming to see to her affairs.3

  3. Believe me, it will not be only this; I know this sister was too free in talking and laughing, and sometimes trouble arises.

  4. So tell her that the Mother is just as pleased; if she wants to come, let her come; that way she can better see to her affairs. If there were a postulant it would be [good]; you can put her in second class by day.4 Try to get them off at once. Put my mind at rest, and goodbye. If you have no money, have it lent to you.5

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Superior had written to her on 4 May that the Sister was worried because her parents, without answering a single word, had sent back a letter of hers asking for information about her dowry.

2 The Mother suggests sending her for a time to the community of S. Martinello (PG), but changes her mind; it is better for her to come to her in Piacenza.

3 She is coming precisely to talk about the dowry.

4 If there were a postulant ready to leave, she could accompany her, in second class.

5 The Superior had no money for the journey.

Grieved at the unpleasant events in the House and worried about the present situation, she urges vigilance in the community and great prudence with outsiders.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I am reading yours, which I received from the sisters, and I am very sorry to hear you tell me that together with that wretched one from Bologna there were others. What? Does that seem a small thing to you? And why do you not tell me at once who the others are, so that they can be removed at once?1 Oh! what days I am going through because of this house!2

2. I tell you in all secrecy that I have received a letter from the Archbishop of Florence.3 Oh! pray and have prayers said; I tell you to look carefully that there are no others, and keep fifty eyes open to watch, when Alessandro comes, that you do not linger at the door. Moreover, the Confessor must always be with you and ser-ved by you.4 In the end, perhaps through your carelessness, I shall have to come to Florence. Oh! Thoughtless ones! Be careful whom you keep in the house!

  1. Do not leave the house; be careful now that the masons are there.5 My God! I have no peace night or day.

  2. The method for playing, that thick music book, wrap it and send it to me;6 there is no need to say anything to anyone.

5. Oh! my God! I tell you, be careful; do all you can to see Canon Ciaranfi and try gently to make him change his mind.7 In short, I am truly on thorns; I cannot tell you what I suffer. In haste, your affectionate M. Rosa

6. Mind the masons; watch carefully what goes on in the house, and say that the work the masons are doing is wanted by the municipality for the schools. Finally, keep watch and tell me who the accomplice sisters are who lent a hand to the t...]8. Goodbye, affectionate Mother

1 Wretched one from Bologna. The Sister who, not entirely sound of mind, had spoken ill of the Superior and the community to the confessor and to the Vicar for Nuns. Cf. L 60,2 and 5. The Mother wants to know who the others in league with the first are. They must be transferred at once.

2 The Florence house continues to cause her worry.

3 Cf. L 60, the reply to the Archbishop's notification to withdraw the Sisters gradually and prudently and finally close the house.

4 the confessor... served. She alone was to receive, serve and finally see out the confessor when he came to the house for his duties. This was to avoid the undue interference that had occurred in the past to the community's harm. Cf. L 55,2.

5 Prudent advice to put an end to the gossip which, carried to the Curia, had caused the Bishop's decision mentioned in n. 3

6 She asks her to send the piano method book.

7 She should try to speak with Canon Luigi Ciaranfi, Vicar for Nuns, and con-vince him prudently of the truth, so that he changes his opinion about the community.

8 The accomplice Sisters she spoke of at the beginning, who lent a hand to the accuser.

She thanks him for accepting the Patronage of the Institute. She encloses a summary of its situation, invites him to visit the Mother House and asks for the final approval of the Constitutions.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. I cannot find words fit to thank Your Most Reverend Eminence for accepting the Patronage of our Poor Institute.1

  2. Allow me humbly to submit a simple summary so that you may see the work the good God has done in so few years; and the requests are so many and of such kinds that I am obliged to refuse them.2

  3. Eminence! If my request were not too bold I would dare to ask you a favour. Before I ask it, cover me with the mantle of your immense charity, bearing with the customs of a wretched daughter of yours, which His Eminence Berardi, of eternal memory to us,3 had granted me: a visit every year here to the Mother House, where I gather all the Superiors in July, the month of Saint Anne, while they make the Holy Exercises given by the Bishop of Piacenza.4 Oh! if this year too I had the good fortune to have my Father Protector, he could see and hear all that is done, and this lowly Servant of the Lord could work with the assurance of pleasing God and Holy Mother Church in all things, as she was assured in the past. Oh! if I could have a line from you granting so signal a favour! may I hope for it? Most Reverend Eminence, your charity makes me hope for everything, and it is what moved me to ask.

  4. Do not forget the poor house at the Parrocchietta, so that they can work in the good season. One word from you and everything will be done with the greatest speed.5

  5. Likewise our Constitutions, which were, one may say, on the eve of being approved; Mgr Bianchi promised me to press

for the final approval; let you but express a wish and we shall have everything as soon as possible.6

6. Forgive the length of my letter while, prostrate at your feet and kissing your hand with veneration, I implore your pastoral blessing upon myself and the Institute, and remain most deeply Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Most humble obedient Daughter Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno

1 The previous Cardinal Protector, Giuseppe Berardi, had died on 6 April 1878.

2 She presents a summary of the Institute's situation regarding its works and adds that requests for others are so many that she must refuse them.

3 ... of eternal memory to us. Cardinal Berardi, whose memory among us will be eternal.

4 Bishop Giambattista Scalabrini.

5 For the Parrocchietta house there was a plan to build the school and the adjoining Sisters' residence in the middle of the vineyard bought for the purpose. In May 1878 Leo XIII approved it and work began. Cf. letters Celsa Speranza to M.Rosa: 2.11.1877; 23.5.1878. The Mother asks the Cardinal to hurry the work along.

6 The Constitutions had been approved ad experimentum in 1874. In 1876 the Institute received the Decree of Praise, and "animadversiones" were put forward regarding the Constitutions. Mgr Bianchi had already taken an interest; it was a matter of pressing for the case to be concluded.

She should go to Mgr Giovannini and ask if he will be extraordinary confessor to the community. Various pieces of advice.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear the sisters are going to Mgr Giovannini's house.1 Ah! for pity's sake send him the best ones, I beg you; go yourself sometimes.2 Everything depends on him; go to him and try to ask whether he would act as your extraordinary confessor. Ask him, and as soon as he says yes I shall write to Rome at once.3 Oh! If that happened it would certainly be a great good for you and for the whole Institute. So do all you can.

  2. You asked me whether you should accept that young woman as a boarder; you may, but not as a sister, since her mind has suffered.4

  3. Never go out except to go to Mgr Giovannini; and meanwhile at night lock them in the house securely.5 If you then see that you cannot be safe, do not stir, for pity's sake.

  4. Oh! what sorrows I have suffered and still suffer! Pray hard, for it is a serious matter.6

Goodbye, in haste, your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Cf. L 51, n. 3; 71,2.

2 She urges her to choose the best Sisters to nurse a sick member of the family at ho-me and to go herself sometimes, at night.

3 The Mother is convinced that if Mgr Giovannini becomes extraordinary confessor to the community he will be able to testify in its favour. Cf. L 71,2.

4 her mind has suffered. She had shown signs of mental weakness.

5 When going out at night to nurse the sick woman she was to take care to lock the doors well.

6 The plots against the Sisters continued. Sr. A. Santina had told her of an understanding between confessor and chaplain, adding: "Mother, I don't want to be in Florence."

She has written to the Archbishop asking him to appoint Mgr Giovannini extraordinary confessor to the community. Various advice on how to deal with the Curia authorities. She should ask the Marchioness to write the Archbishop a letter about the running of the house and the Sisters' work.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received yours1 and assure you it relieved me a little. I immediately wrote a letter of thanks to Mgr Giovannini and also to the Archbishop in Rome asking him to grant him to us as extraordinary confessor; and then he must keep him for good, no longer the one you have, [who] unfortunately has said and done plenty.2

  2. Go to Ciaranfi too, for I assure you he has done something; and so if you could rid yourself of that old man, who seeks nothing but to talk. Oh! how much he says and, worse, does.3

  3. So, if by misfortune they said to you: "You cannot stay here any longer", answer: "I know nothing; I receive my orders from Piacenza; when they think they want something, let them wri-te there; nothing was done for us to be so ill-treated."4 Enough: politely, but always firmly.

  4. As soon as either of us learns anything about having Mgr Giovannini as extraordinary confessor, write to me at once, at once.

5. Stay always close to the Marchioness;5 she can do everything, and certainly if she would write a line to the Archbishop about how pleased she is with the House and its good running and the nursing for which you are so much in demand!

6. Without telling her anything, you could say to her: "Marchioness, there are many who persecute us and keep speaking ill of us to the Archbishop, saying that nothing is done.6 Would you write him a couple of lines? We are your daughters; tell him how well we are doing, the sick, and show him

that you have many, and also the schools and the boarders." I shall write to thank her for what she does, but you, politely, ask her to do something.

7. Keep watch always, night and day, so that Mgr Giovannini is always pleased with what the nurses do; see that they do it well, observe them in everything. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 In the L of the 11th she reported the visit to Mgr Giovannini and his willingness to accept the office of extraordinary confessor, subject to the Curia's authorization.

2 Grant him to us in place of the one you have, who has not been favourable to you.

3 Go to... does. She should therefore go to the Vicar for Nuns, Luigi Ciaranfi, who has somewhat changed his mind and is trying to free the community from the chaplain, who was also hostile to it.

4 ill-treated: badly treated and judged.

5 The Marchioness Carolina Covoni was a benefactress of the Sisters; she esteemed and helped them.

6 ... saying that nothing is done. One of the accusations carried to the Archbishop, the most se-rious, was this: the Daughters of Saint Anne do nothing in the Diocese. The Archbishop himself had cited it as a valid reason for closing the house: "as presently constituted (the Institute) cannot produce in my Diocese the good that it seemed to at first." Cf. L 60, n. 3.

Advice on the running of the house and the professional training of a Sister. She asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am exceedingly tired and have an abyss of business to finish, so tell the sisters, both the Superior and the other, that I am answering you for all. 1

2. As for the Superior, I cannot believe that 1,200 F. a year is not enough for her, I cannot believe it, so I do not allow you to add anything.2

  1. As for the sister: let us hope she can get her diploma there and become a little quicker and more capable;3 so when you have had the examinations you will come here.4 The superior will come first for the Holy Exercises; she will be told by a couple of lines. As for the piano, that is fine.5

  2. I see that you too are of my opinion about not spending money on other people's houses, for it would be real folly, and so far away besides. Listen, you tell me you have 500 F.; you could send them to me in an insured packet by post; I would need them; see that you insure them properly.

  3. Pray to Mary for me and for the Institute, for a grace is wanted soon.6 So see that all the prayers are offered for my intention.

Goodbye, dear Daughter; the months pass quickly, so soon you will be with me. Yours for all ages, my affectionate M. Rosa

1 The superior: Sr. A. Elisa Corsini; the other is Sr. A. Fabia De Giorgi.

2 The Superior considered £.1,200 a year insufficient for the community and asked for something extra from the income of the school for adult women, which was reserved as a subsidy for the Mother House.

3 Sr. A. Fabia had sat the diploma examinations and failed arithmetic. The Mother wants her to take the resit in Maratea.

4 She refers to the pupils' end-of-year examinations.

5 A piano was to be bought. Sr. A. Irene was putting aside money from some offerings.

6 The grace desired: a favourable solution to the problem of the Florence house.

She tells her she wishes to come to Florence for a brief, secret meeting with Mgr Giovannini.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. A line in all secrecy; for pity's sake, don't let Alessandro know. Listen, if you do not betray me I shall stop for a few hours to speak with Mgr Giovannini, but woe to you if you betray me.2 You must say nothing to Alessandro, and first you must assure me that there will be no danger of his seeing me.

  2. And you will send no more sisters, but go to him yourself, for you will hear everything in person.3 I await a letter from you at once here in Pistoia, at once, so that on Tuesday by the first train I would be with you.4 What do you say? I await yours and am

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The date is deduced from the context and particularly from her unexpected trip to Florence.

2 Having decided to stay in Florence only a few hours to discuss the serious problem of the Florence work with Mgr Attilio Giovannini, she absolutely does not want her son to know she is there.

3 The Sisters went to his house to nurse a sick woman. The service was to be suspended. She was, however, to tell him of her arrival.

4 She reached Florence on the 18th and had to stay. Cf. L 68,1. She left again on 31 May.

She sets out the problem of the Florence house and asks him to intervene on behalf of the Institute.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. I hope you will have read my letter, which I sent you through a Sister with the summary of the Institute enclosed. 1 Now I am in great dis-tress over a trial that has arisen here in Florence, where I had to come yesterday because of certain slanders and truly foolish falsehoods carried to the Curia, in which I can assure you there is nothing true.2

  2. But first of all allow me to tell you frankly that the confessor is at the bottom of everything, because he would like to make an enclosed convent, and finding himself opposed he stirs up all sorts of trouble;3 and finally, there being a Sister whose convulsions left her mind a little weak and who decided she wanted to go home, he received her in his own house, then took her to the Vicariate, telling the Superior she was there; and she went to fetch her and took her to Piacenza.4

  3. On the strength of this he claimed there was not enough supervision, adding a thousand foolish things, all of which I can assure you he invented; and in confession he does nothing but speak ill of the Superiors to the Sisters, trying to make them lose their vocation. The worst is that the Vicar for Nuns believes him.5

  4. Your Most Reverend Eminence well knows that we are in no way bound to submit to internal direction from the confessor. He is only to hear confessions and nothing else.

  5. For now I add nothing more. If things get worse I am resolved to come to your feet and tell you in person, in all truth, how matters stand; and Your Most Reverend Eminence will surely de-

fend your work and save your poorest Daughter, who asks your pastoral blessing and, prostrate, remains Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Most humble obedient Daughter Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 It is L 63.

2 Cf. L 60

3 Cf. L 55,2 and notes.4Cf. L 62,1.

4 Cf. L 62,1.

5 Cf. L 62,5.

She should invite the new Cardinal Protector to visit the house.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Go at once to invite Cardinal Franchi, beg him to come,1 and do what Mgr Negrotto tells you about the villa.2 God alone knows how many letters to the Protector and how many steps our agent has taken, and finally.

  2. Enough, dear daughter, I add nothing more, I am so busy. Goodbye; greet everyone for me, and Sr. A. Crocifissa and the other,3

your affectionate M. Rosa

Pray, and tell Crocifissa; I am not well.

1 the new Cardinal Protector. Cf. L 63.

2 On the same day work had begun on the new school and Sisters' residence. Cf. L 63,4, n. 5.

3 ... and the other: Sr. A. Pudenziana Farossi.

Grieved by the slanders, new every day, against the Sisters' work, which are reported to the Archbishop, still in Rome, she assures him that in six days she has seen for herself perfect order and observance in the house and growth and flourishing in its educational and nursing work. He should put in a good word with the Archbishop.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. How grieved I am and what cruel torment my soul suffers I cannot express, under a weight of slanders which they devise anew every day and then write to the Archbishop, who is there.

  2. Ah, for pity's sake, Most Reverend Eminence, say a word to Monsignor the Archbishop1 and assure him that what he has been told is not true. As for the slanders I have heard, I can likewise assure you in all truth that in these six days I have been in this house,2 having made the most minute observations on the good keeping of both the rules and the timetable, everything proceeds in the most exact order.

  3. The schools are very numerous, the boarding school is growing, and as for the sick, there are so many requests that some must be refused every day.

  4. If Your Most Reverend Eminence thinks I should come to Rome, write and tell me, and I shall obey at once; I would have done so already, but my poor health has prevented me, which these days, by God's mercy, I suffer more than usual.

  5. Most Reverend Eminence! Send me a word from you to calm me, for I have extreme need of it.3 Blessed God will repay you a hundredfold with his graces for the charity you show this poor Servant of yours.

Prostrate at your feet she implores your pastoral blessing, while full of veneration I am Your Most Reverend Eminence's most obedient Daughter Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 Archbishop Eugenio Cecconi was in Rome.

2 She had arrived on the 18th of this month.

3 He replied on 29 May, comforting her and assuring her of his intervention with the Archbishop.

Because of the slanders already mentioned, the Archbishop has ordered the Sisters withdrawn from Florence. She begs him to defend his Daughters. She invites him to the Mother House.

Most Reverend Eminence,

1. I cannot express the sorrow I feel at seeing that, on account of such foolish slanders,1 Archbishop Cecconi has pronounced an unwelcome sentence, namely that we should leave his Diocese and withdraw.2 My God! for such trifling things, and, to tell the whole truth, the pique of a [...]!!!

2. Moreover our Parish Priest, a most distinguished person, Mgr Giovannini, parish priest of San Lorenzo, is ready to provide any testimonial, both for the nursing and for the schools, and he has sometimes also been confessor.3

  1. Eminence! because one person wrote to the Archbishop whatever they thought fit, must the poor Institute be allowed to suffer such a humiliation?

  2. Your power, joined to your great shrewdness in doing good, will surely take up the defence of your Daughters.

  3. Most Reverend Eminence! Ah, for pity's sake, a single line from you to relieve my anxiety. I should be returning to the Mother House. May I go in peace? I no longer speak of coming to Rome,4 because I cannot stand the heat and would do nothing but come and take to my bed; I am suffering greatly.

  4. Oh! If I could have you in Piacenza and tell you so many, many things, Eminence! May I hope for it? Do this charity. My God! Am I too bold? Just one word with your pastoral blessing, while prostrate at your feet I remain Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Obedient Daughter Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 Foolish. Cf. L 70,1.

2 He had already written to her to withdraw the Sisters gradually. Cf. L 60.3Cf. L 65,1.

4 Cf. L 70,4.

She has been told that the Town Council wants to give the Sisters' residence over to the military. She orders her to leave everything and come away.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. From your telegram, that the Council wants the house for the soldiers.1 Well then, (I) it seems a very good thing for you all to come here; and be sure to take away everything, everything, for perhaps it will be a fine excuse. All for the best.

  2. So ask the Council to let you hold the examinations earlier. Oh! how much better that will be! Tell Sr. A. Sempliciana2 that I have prepared some fine work for her; so be quick, there is enough for all. Goodbye; write at once whether you will be with me by the 15th. Goodbye.

Your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The telegram had been sent by the Council. The Superior for her part explains what it is about.
