Two regiments were to stop at Varallo, so the Council, having to find quarters and knowing that every year all the Sisters went to Piacenza for a month, had proposed that the Superior give up the house for that period. They would have stored the furniture safely in one room and would have paid the Sisters £.75 rent. The Superior said she was pleased; with that money she would have paid off the debts.

2 Sr. A. Sempliciana Saviotti, the teacher.

Advice about the house and a Sister.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Listen, going to Don Bosco's nuns is no fault, indeed you did well;1 but the disobedience was letting the Sister write to that Friar, when I had told you that you must not allow her to write to anyone.2

  2. Oh! what did it matter if you had received the telegram;3 you should have taken no notice of it. Oh! why not do as I told you? So the Friar will have come to you there, and what did you do? Did you let her speak with him alone? Oh! what disobedience! Be more careful and do what I told you.

Goodbye. I am your affectionate M. Rosa

This is the table you are to use for the six-monthly accounts, and then keep the form for the next six your [M. Rosa]

1 Nothing to object to in the visit to Don Bosco's Sisters, but she disobe-yed in the rest.

2 The letters it answers are missing, so there is no information to understand fully.

3 what did it matter = what difference did it make. You should have disregarded it.

She asks for prayers for two problems causing her great suffering.

Dear friend,

1. Listen, I really need you to tell that dear Soul you know of;1 ask her whether the affair I am handling is God's will,2 and also what will become of the rules, for they never come out.3 Have prayers said and pray. Oh! how weighed down I am with sorrows! Tell me whether they will end and how. Under obedience, tell me what I ask.

2. Do you know that poor Fr Richino has died?4 Oh! how he suffered, just as you said! And what is dear Rosa doing? Tell me something.

Thank you for all you do for the Sisters. May Saint Anne reward you, your affectionate friend Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The dear soul, Rosa Parodi, a young friend of Anna's, who died in the odour of sanctity. Cf. Lettere 1, p. 524.

2 That affair. The problem of the Florence house, for which she was fight-ing so as not to withdraw the Sisters. Cf. L 167, n. 1.

3 She had also appealed to Cardinal Franchi about the Rules. Cf. L 63,5.

4 "Fr Richino", Fr Antonio Accinelli had written to her on 28 May, "is at the point of death; he has already received extreme unction; they tell me he is suffering greatly." He recovered, however. He died on 25.9.1878. Cf. L Accinelli 26.9.1878 to M. Rosa. Cf. Lettere 1, p. 529.

She informs him that she has already asked the Bishops for letters of "commendation". She asks for news of the Rules and expresses concern for the Florence House. She encloses a testimonial from the Chaplain.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. I reply by return of post to your most venerated letter, deeply grieved to be a cause of displeasure to Your Most Reverend Eminence1 instead of bringing you consolation with news of the good progress of the work which Your Most Reverend Eminence protects with such charity and kindness! Alas, my wretchedness reduces the affairs of a holy work, which cost the good God infinitely, to this state!!

  2. Your Most Reverend Eminence tells me to provide myself with letters of Commendation?2 These have already been delivered twice to the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars: the first time when we had the decree of praise, the second in '77 for the final approval of the Rules;3 and among these was also that of the Archbishop of Florence; the last was from the end of '77, and it was very fine. I am sorry I did not keep a copy, as I did of so many others that passed through my hands; I lack several, because they were addressed to the Congregation, but His Eminence, of eternal memory, told me he had read them and that they were very fine, beyond our merits. If Your Most Reverend Eminence would like a copy of those I have, I shall send them at once.

  3. I hear that the Rules are once again at the Holy Office.4 I really cannot understand why, when poor Cardinal Berardi had worked on them so much! Most Reverend Eminence! what can it mean? Oh! if I could speak to you, and you could examine everything with your own eyes as poor Berardi did, this lowly creature would surely come away assured that under the heavy yoke God has laid on me everything is pleasing to Him and to the Catholic Church;5 even

though the suffering is such!!!! But for me to come to Rome?! my God! I scarcely have the strength to stand!!

  1. Allow me to transcribe what the Archbishop said to our Bishop of Piacenza: "I must uphold what I said, because in Florence they say I am not in command; so I stand firm on what I said." What sort of reasons are these? So, to show that he is in command? My God!

  2. I have written to the Parish Priest for his testimonial, and I enclose one from the Chaplain, and I know that others have written to the Archbishop.6 I am writing to him again myself; I did not dare to do so any more because he had me told not to write to him again.7

  3. I close because I am very unwell; I prostrate myself at your feet and humbly ask your pastoral blessing, while with the greatest veneration I remain Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Most humble obedient Daughter Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The letter received is dated 5 June. He writes that he had commended her cause to the Archbishop of Florence and had been "surprised and disheartened" by his explanations.

2 He wrote to her verbatim: "... I hasten to urge you... to come to a perfect understanding with the said eminent Prelate and to find a way of obtaining his support, no less than that of the other Ordinaries, on behalf of your houses".

3 Letters of "commendation" had been requested and received from the Bishops in 1875 to obtain recognition of the Institute, whose Decree of Praise was granted by the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars on 4 April 1876. A second set of commendations was obtained in 1877.

4 Cf. L 63, n. 6.

5 If I could speak to you... Church. She had already invited him to the Mother House, where he would have seen the reality of the Institute for himself.

6 The parish priest: Mgr Attilio Giovannini; the chaplain, Fr Baldassarre Fini. She encloses a report from the latter.

7 She writes the same day. It is L 76.

She apologizes for daring to write to him. She humbles herself and asks pardon for "the house", assuring him that the charges against the Sisters are slanders.

Most Reverend Excellency,

  1. Although I realize it is almost insolent to dare to send you my writings,1 I also know well that, as the Pastor of a distinguished Diocese, an office you fill so wisely, I cannot help thinking that by prostrating myself at your feet and begging you I shall still find the Father and benefactor I had for three whole years.

  2. Correct me, punish me, if it is I who have given cause for that poor house to be struck by so great a punishment.2 Ah! for pity's sake, pardon the house and punish (me) myself; tell me what I have done and I am ready to do penance for it.

  3. I would have flown to your feet in Rome, but I reached Florence and then the fever would not leave me, and I had to turn back, although I am still very ill; certainly it would be good for the work that...3 May God do with me as he wills.

  4. Mgr Giovannini has promised to put in a word too. Most Reverend Excellency, believe me, the charges about the house are slanders. As for me, oh! I am an abyss of wretchedness!!! Unworthy even to be a Christian. Alas! poor servant of the Lord!4

5. A word of pardon for the house, punishment for me; I prostrate myself at your feet as I ask your pastoral blessing, and with bowed head remain, with veneration,

Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most humble devoted Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

I enclose a copy of Fini's.5

1 He had let her know that it was useless to write to him again. Cf. L 75,5.

2 The punishment, that is, the closure.

3 ... I had to turn back. After thirteen days in Florence she had to return to Piacenza, on 31 May. It would be good for the work that. She does not finish the sentence. Perhaps she meant: that the Lord should take me to himself. But she corrects herself with an act of full abandonment to God's will.

4 Unworthy... Lord. Expressions of deep humility, arising not from this passing situation of difficulty and discouragement but from her constant imitation of her Master: "Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart." Mt 11:29.

5 The copy of the chaplain's testimonial, also sent to Cardinal Franchi. Cf. L 75, n. 6.

She suggests she seek Mgr Giovannini's advice on how to deal with the Vicar and the Curia.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Listen, go to Mgr Giovannini and say to him: "Mother sends me here so that you may tell me how I should proceed, both for the retreat and for a little instruction for the Sisters; I shall do as you say." Ask whether you should go to Ciaranfi, in short how you should deal with the Curia.1

  2. For the rest, let us pray. The devil does his utmost, but Jesus is all-powerful. In His month he will not fail to help us.2

Goodbye. Yours in haste. Accept the postulant and send her when you like. Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Listen... Curia. Ask too whether you should go to the Vicar for Nuns, Ciaranfi; in short, how to behave with the clergy of the Curia.

2 "Prayer is the key to all graces": she knows it from experience. Jesus is the strongest. She hopes for everything from Him in the month of June, consecrated to Him.

She sends him a testimonial from Mgr Attilio Giovannini as evidence of the slanders against the Sisters of the Florence house. She repeats her invitation to come to Piacenza.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. I have just received the letter of Mgr Giovannini, Parish Priest of San Lorenzo in Florence, whom I had asked for a certificate. He answers in the terms Your Most Reverend Eminence will see from his letter, which I enclose, keeping a copy. Believe me, Eminence, they are all slanders.2 I am also told that they have now turned everything against me. For this I bless God, so long as the Lord's Work suffers nothing. There are 52 houses, and never in twelve years has anything like this happened, and all of them, by God's mercy, are doing well.

  2. Eminence! Make the sacrifice of coming here, so that you can examine everything carefully and punish me if you find things I have not done well.3 Yesterday the Bishop told me there was every likelihood that Your Most Reverend Eminence would come among us. He would like to know when, and I too join him in begging you to let us know, so that I can gather all the Superiors and Your Most Reverend Eminence will hear from them how things are going, and the Bishop will give them the Holy Exercises.

  3. And meanwhile this unworthy servant of the Lord is pressing and will press earnestly to be relieved of the burden I drag along so poorly, and I shall cease to be a stumbling block4 to greater good, always obedient to submit to any toil and glad to give my last breath for the Work of My God.5

4. A line from you; I hope to obtain everything from your charity,6 while I prostrate myself at your feet asking your pastoral blessing, and with the greatest veneration remain Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Most humble obedient Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The date is deduced from that of the letter she forwards: 8 June 1878.

2 In his testimonial Mgr Giovannini says: "the whole thing is stirred up in a mystery of accusations."

3 She had invited him earlier, on 7 June, expressing her wish to speak to him. Cf. L 75, n. 5.

4 ... relieved of the burden, of the office of superior general.

5 ... always obedient... breath. Her readiness is total: she has offered herself as a victim for God's Work.

6 ... I hope to obtain everything. Sadly the Lord's ways were otherwise. Cardinal Franchi died little more than a month later, on 31 July 1878.

She asks for news of her mother. She asks her to go and visit the house at Sestri.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, I would like to know what Mamma said.1 Another thing: go to Sestri for a while, have a look and then write to me.2 For your information, I shall be away from Piacenza for four days; say nothing. Goodbye, I am in haste, your affectionate for all ages

Affectionate M. Rosa

1 Mother Rosa's mother was unwell and wanted to see her daughter. Fr Antonio Accinelli had told her so.

2 When necessary the Mother entrusted her with visiting the houses at Sestri and Sampierdarena.

She advises her to keep the savings with her and hand them over in person.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear from yours about your cash box; God be blessed.1 Keep it all with you and bring it to me when you come. The Superior would like you to give her some; she tells me she cannot manage; is it true?2 I don't believe it; I leave it all to your judgement, for I put little faith in what she tells me.3

  2. The months pass quickly, the days fly and we shall see each other. Carla sends greetings, the nurse thanks you, and so does Carla. In haste, I am for all ages

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Sister was the community bursar. She had put aside a certain sum.

2 The Superior wanted to spend that money on the house.

3 She advises her to use her own judgement.

Two Sisters are coming. She writes a warning for them, to be read to them in secret.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to tell you that two Sisters will arrive from Terricciola,2 and you, in all confidence, for no one must know, will read them these two lines alone, shut in your room, as soon as they arrive.

2. Daughters,

I warn you that if you two say anything to the Sisters about what, because of you, gave rise to murmuring in the house where you were, I tell you that as soon as I hear of it your veil will be taken away without pity or pardon. So you must speak neither well nor ill of the house where you have been.3 Woe to you! Your affectionate M. Rosa

3. Do me the kindness of keeping them a few days without letting them go out,4 and watch them all the time, and then write to me. As for Sr. A. Lucia, I shall move her soon;5 be patient. My God! These are real torments! Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

1 This L bears the date 1870 but cannot belong to that time, for several reasons. First, because the correspondent had not yet entered the Institute (she entered in 1875), nor had the Terricciola house been opened, which dates from 1874. It is rather to be assigned to 1878 on the basis of elements clearly stated in the correspondence of Sr. A. Amabile (cf. letters to M. Rosa) and of Sr. A. Beatrice Merici about the events at Terricciola (cf. letters to M. Rosa June 1878).

2 The two Sisters: Sr. A. Bonaventura and Sr. A. Ildegarda.

3 che voi siete state: where you have been.

4 sortire: go out.

5 "Sr. A. Lucia is doing everything to get away from Genoa", Sr. A. Amabile writes to M. Rosa on 16.6.1878.

She sends him a letter from the Provincial of the Piarists.

Most Reverend Eminence,

1. I received the enclosed several days ago;1 I delayed sending it because I would first have liked a line from you in answer to my registered letter.2

2. Impart your pastoral blessing to your most afflicted daughter, who prostrates herself at your feet and with the greatest veneration remains Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Most humble obedient Daughter Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The letter of Fr Mauro Ricci of the Pious Schools, a Florentine and a famous writer. From 1886 until his death (1900) he was General of his Congregation. 2L 78.

2 L 78, of 9-10 June of this year.

She tells her a Sister is coming. Encouragement and advice about the community.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Sr. A. Beatrice will be coming to Florence; if you have postulants ready, send them with her, if she has some with her.1 Send her on at once and make sure she does not go to confession to anyone,2 but send her here at once.

  2. Matters there are still quiet and I hope they will come to an end,3 but believe me, before that there will still be some fine trials to go through.

  3. Let us pray, for the devil is at work; but we must really storm the Heart of Jesus, and then observance, and you will see that Cepinetto will have to go.

  4. Look after the sisters; tell them to pray, and that I greet them all and always remember the lovely days I spent with them at recreation;4 but now is a time for work; tell them to pray that I may have strength to do what is so necessary.

Your affectionate M. Rosa in haste

1 Sr. A. Beatrice Merici would pass through Florence. She could send off in her company {send them with her) the postulants who were ready, and her own too, if she had any ready.

2 "... not go to confession to anyone." The Mother feared that some Florentine pri-est might tell her what had happened in the Florence house.

3 Matters there are still quiet. It seems they are no longer talked about. Cf. L 82, nn. 1-2.

4 The Mother had stayed with the community from 18 to 31 May.

She encloses Mgr A. Giovan-nini's letter. The Bishop of Piacenza too has written to Archbishop Cecconi. She renews her invitation to the Mother House.

Most Reverend Eminence,

1. I cannot tell you how it pains me to have to trouble you continually with these tiresome letters of mine, always about the Florence affair.2 Having written again to Mgr Giovannini, as well as to the Father Provincial of the Piarists,3 to obtain some testimonial about that house, Mgr Giovannini has answered me, and I enclose his letter. Please keep it, Your Most Reverend Eminence.

2. The Bishop of Piacenza has already written three times to the Archbishop of Florence, the last time yesterday, very forcefully, and he said he would write today to Your Most Reverend Eminence too, since certain heads of accusation have reached me that are truly false, utterly false, and I see no point in transcribing them, for they are worthless.4

  1. Deign to impart your pastoral blessing to me, that it may give me strength to stay on my feet, just as I felt great relief on receiving your most venerated letter, although there was no word in it to make me hope I might have you here.5

  2. I am truly indiscreet and too bold, but I also know well that so great a favour is obtained only by unceasing entreaty. As I prostrate myself and with the greatest veneration kiss your hand, I remain Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Obedient Daughter Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The date is deduced from that of the letter she sends him for information.

2 The Florence affair. Cf. L 68; 70; 71; 76; 78.

3 Mgr Attilio Giovannini, parish priest of San Lorenzo. Cf. L 78. The Father Provincial of the Piarists, Celestino Zini.

4 "The accusations", Mgr Giovannini specified in his letter of 18 June, "concern not so much the Florence house as the whole Institute".

5 She had invited him to Piacenza. Cf. L 78,2.

She answers her about the prizes to be given to the schoolgirls.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, you tell me you have to give the prizes.1 Tell me how it is and whether it is meant for the municipal Schools. If it is for these, no; if it is for yours and you believe you really are obliged, then do it.2

2. Oh! I cannot wait to see you, and then we can settle things better. Please be economical. I think I have answered everything. In haste, your affectionate M. Rosa

1 She had written to her on 17 June that "the Committee and the Mayor" had said they should see to the end-of-year prize-giving.

2 The girls' section of the municipal Schools was run by the Daughters of Saint Anne. The teaching Sisters had to prepare prizes for the pupils of this school.

Various advice: she should send the Sisters out collecting alms and let a Sister go to Genoa for the baths. She should use her judgement in certain "little things" in the house. She should buy bedspreads for the boarders.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Yesterday I received your letter. As for the postulant, do as you think best; as for the Confessor, always do as Mgr Giovannini tells you.1 For the alms collection send the ones we had agreed on, for they seem good to me.

2. Listen, if for the moment they cannot go to the sick, we must be patient;2 it is enough that you can send them out collecting at once and gather a good store for the winter. Then you will be less worried and need send them out less, won't you? Matters are still the same, but: victory is written in Heaven, so courage, and for pity's sake, observance.3

  1. Listen, send that gossip to Genoa;4 see whether you can send her here if need be, and then I shall send her for the baths. Oh! my God! one wonders whether there were baths in her own home! But see that the Doctor himself says when she should leave, otherwise it looks as if they are dying. My God! perhaps in the middle of a field on straw they were better off. How dreadful!

  2. Use your own judgement in certain little things. Listen, as for the teacher, I really don't know what to do;5 it was good that you did not keep Sr. A. Maria, for she is scatterbrained.

  3. I hear what the confessor is doing, and certainly it is a very serious matter; enough.6 I mean serious as regards the Confessor; for the rest all is well. Tell the Marchioness to go ahead and buy the bedspreads, for there is no dan-

ger.7 Always behave as you have done, so that no one can find fault. Goodbye, in haste, your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Mgr Giovannini had advised her to invite the confessor to give the Sisters the in-struction on the day of recollection.

2 The Confessor had advised the Superior not to take on nursing of the sick.

3 She refers to the familiar problem of the house.

4 A Sister was insisting on going to Genoa for the baths.

5 The lay teacher was not competent. Sr. A. Santina regretted it and asked for a Sister teacher.

6 The confessor kept giving advice on the running of the house.

7 Tell the Marchioness Carolina Covoni to buy the white bedspreads for the boarding school, since there is no longer any danger of the house being closed.

She announces the arrival of the Sisters for the alms collection.

A.M.F.

Dear Daughter,

1. I am well ahead with the work. The Sister who hands you this letter, for pity's sake, must not talk with the others. I mean, keep an eye on her so that she does not go out. You know, she is a bit of a featherbrain.2 I shall come myself and then see to it. Greetings to all; yours in my dear Crucified One

affectionate M. Rosa

Give her a white coffee. Two are going to Pisa.3

The date is deduced from the context.

Featherbrain, rather thoughtless and talkative.

She refers to the Sisters going to Pisa to collect alms.

She answers her correspondent, who is distressed and "without peace" because her parents are "angry" with her. She gives her the example of Jesus in the temple, urging her to sublimate her love for her relatives.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I received your dear letter and hear of the pain you feel over your relatives according to the flesh.2 When his most holy Mother reproached Jesus for staying behind in the temple without telling her,3 and so causing her great pain and distress, what did this dear Love answer her? "I came to do the will of my Eternal Father. He is my Mother and my Father".4 Can any sorrow compare with this of Mary's: to have lost Jesus, the sole object of her love, the sole comfort of her heart?

  2. Tell me, blessed daughter: when in those days of dryness we do not feel him, we no longer have the sweetness of him that we taste!? Tell me, tell me, what must Mary have felt?

  3. Oh! father and mother according to the flesh! St Francis, our father, called them a plague of the soul, because they always infect it with something carnal and rob our poor soul of the beauty and sublimity with which Jesus adorned it at such cost.5

  4. I don't know what to say, daughter; yes, I shall let you see them, you will satisfy them.6 Alas! that I should be the channel of the plague to infect my little angel, mine, in you, Jesus, who gave her to me. She is pure and so I want to keep her.

  5. Answer me and tell me whether you felt nothing to offer to Jesus.7 Oh! sacrifice of Abraham, which made you Father of the living!!

Your affectionate M. for all ages affectionate M. R.

1 The Sister's letter exists, but undated. The present one is assumed to belong to this period for several reasons: Sr. A. Veneranda had been Superior at Toceno for only a few months, found the task difficult and was discouraged. Cf. L 50,1. Her request to see her parents again, who were "angry" at her leaving without their consent, could be granted by the Mother, not least because the schools would close at the end of June.

2 She had written: "In the midst of the greatest desolation... thinking that my parents are angry, I can no longer find peace".

3 Her parents reproached the Sister for having had her own way, leav-ing Genoa to enter the FSA in Piacenza.

4Cf. Lk 2:41-50.

5 Detachment from relatives is the fruit and consequence of the fundamental option: to follow Christ in the Gospel radicalism of detachment from everything.

6 I don't know what to say... satisfy them. The Mother seems uncertain but gives, albeit reluctantly, a positive answer: yes, I shall let you see them, you will satisfy them. And great was the joy of those parents, for the following August their daughter was transferred to Naples and visited her family first.

7 Answer me... "I take in all you tell me, and I thank you...".

She comforts and encourages her.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I have received yours and hear that you still cannot get free of the examinations.1 Patience and courage, and don't take it so hard; take heart, everything comes to an end. Away, away with melancholy, which, as you know, is the Devil's net.2 Courage, good wine, and goodbye.

I am so, so busy that I don't know whether I am coming or going; yours for ever

affectionate M. Rosa

1 In her letter of 26 June she wrote that it was impossible to bring the examinations forward because of local circumstances. The pupils had been absent for over a month to work in the vineyards. The examinations took place on 28 and 29 July.

2 Sr. A. Gesuina is under treatment, and "living apart" makes her "melancholy".

Recommendations about the ordinary and extraordinary confessors. Some notices.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received yours and reply by return of post. Listen, send the Sisters again to confession to Mgr Gio-vannini and add the old one as well; 1 tell her to tell him everything she told you, and what the confessor said to her, everything. And then let those few go there;2 if he says anything you can answer that what is done is done with the Curia's permission, and nothing more.3

  2. Courage, good manners, but confide in no one; so be firm both with the C... and with the Confessor.4 Go to Mgr Giovannini, tell him the sisters beg you not to send them, and tell him everything you wrote to me, everything, everything. Let us pray; God is powerful and will defend his work.

  3. The Masses you sent me,5 which the Chaplain said, are they the ones I gave him the money for, or are they to be paid? Find out; try to pay him for them; for pity's sake we must swallow it,6 you understand me.

  4. Goodbye. I am in haste; for your information: on Monday I leave and shall be back on Thursday or Wednesday; I am going to Borgo7 and Bologna and Ferrara, then Piacenza. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Send again to confession to Mgr Giovannini (the community's extraordinary confessor) the Sisters who had preferred him to the ordinary confessor, and add the oldest Sister too, telling her to re-peat to him what she told you about the questions on the running of the house that the ordinary confessor had improperly put to her. Cf. L 68.

2 Let those few go to confession to the ordinary confessor.

3 ... and nothing more. Without adding further explanations.

4 with the C: with the chaplain.

5 sent entered in the accounts.

6 swallow it: put up with it perforce.

7 Borgo S. Donnino, now Fidenza. She was accompanying the five Sisters who were beginning service at the hospital. Cf. Ind. IV.

She asks her to explain to Canon Bia-gini how his brother had come to learn of a secret.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A hasty line to tell you to go to the Canon1 and tell him everything, and tell him you said nothing, nothing; only that, he having lost Andreotti's letter,2 the maid picked it up and gave it to his brother.3 In short, you must tell him everything; for pity's sake don't let him be offended. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Canon Angelo Biagini

2 Ottavio Andreotti, his friend and a benefactor of the Institute, had surely written him something about the inheritance.

3 to the Canon's brother. The corresponding letters are missing and nothing precise can be inferred. Cf. L 27.

Advice and news about the house.

A.M.F.

Dear Daughter,

  1. I received yours with the accounts and am working to see about making bread at home there too;2 as for wine, two big casks will come; likewise for the leaves3 I shall send you money as soon as I can.

  2. I assure you that when I received that letter I felt very ill to see that through two thoughtless heads the notes would have been lost.4 Oh! Goodbye, yours in my dear Crucified One

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The date is deduced from the context.

2 By the following 6 July bread was already being made at home in the Florence house. Cf. L Santina of 6.7.78 to M. Rosa.

3 The leaves: maize husks for filling the straw mattresses.

4 There is no information to understand the matter.

She explains what is needed for the acceptance of two postulants.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. A line in reply to yours; tell that priest1 that I have received no letter, and tell him I shall do all I can to accept them, but I need to know what they have, both as to dowry and age, surname; and that they must have all their papers and trousseau and the dowry.2 In short, let him write me everything clearly and I shall answer at once.

  2. As for the confessor, I think it will be all right.3 Oh! Yes, one day everything will come to light and you will see that it will all end well, it is certain.4 It is observance that brings every good; it is disorder that brings houses down.

  3. Goodbye. Listen, I said I had received nothing from this priest who speaks of the postulants, but it may have arrived while I was away5 and the Superior answered it. But if it was inside yours, no, because no one opens my letters. Goodbye. Your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 A Religious had put forward two postulants.

2 The Mother specifies what is needed for acceptance: personal details, age, documents, trousseau, dowry.

3 It will be good to continue as she told her: leave the Sisters free to go to confession to the ordinary or the extraordinary confessor. Cf. L 90,1-2.

4 Light will be shed on all the rumours and slanders against the community. Cf. L 167.

5 On 1 July the Mother had left Piacenza. Cf. L 90,4.

Two novices are coming who are assigned to Terricciola.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. These two Novices are assigned to Terricciola; as soon as they are rested and refreshed1 send them off to Terricciola, telling them that as soon as they reach Pontedera station they should stop and at once take a carriage to Terricciola. It would be good to send them off in the morning so that they arrive early.

  2. Listen, you do well to hold the examinations soon, and so we shall see the last of that Sberufu!1 and then I shall see to it. Be careful that nothing happens during the Holy Exercises. As for you, for now patience is needed and you must stay.3

  3. They write from Terricciola asking you to get them some sacks to send you the wheat; try to arrange to have a good supply.4

  4. Do everything as Mgr Giovannini tells you. Tell him the Piarists keep insisting that we come to an agreement with Ciaranfi and the Vicar; ask him whether you should go there, and hear what he says.5 For the rest, be cheerful, for everything will end well.6

  5. How is providence going? Write me something. Are girls coming? Goodbye, your

affectionate M. Rosa

Refreshed, restored.

2 Sberufu, a Genoese expression. The lay teacher was unsuitable. Cf. L 86, n. 5.

3 The Sisters were to make the Spiritual Exercises. She, for the moment, had to stay at home.

4 Two Sisters had gone to Terricciola to collect wheat.

5 The Piarist Fathers of Florence advised her to come to an agreement with Mgr Ciaranfi and the Vicar. It was best to follow the opinion of Mgr Attilio Gio-vannini.

6 She refers to the problems of the house. Cf. L 76.

Notices about some Sisters. Carlotta and her family will arrive with Sr. A. Benedetta. She forbids her to send her fish.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You will hear from the sister my intentions about the sick ones. Listen, try to persuade them to go home; and so that bad one, out.1

  1. Listen, if you need nurses write to me at once and I shall send you some; be of good heart.

  2. Carla will come on Monday with Sr. A. Benedetta, the Little Doll and Gaspare, and as soon as I have cleared my desk I shall come too.

  3. Today I received the Saint,2 which is so beautiful, and with it the fish; but for your information, don't [send me any]; I don't eat them and they are always thrown away. Enough, I don't want them because I find them repugnant.3 Goodbye. I am your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Mother's intentions. She had assigned to the Genoa community, a house of nurses, some novices of delicate health and unsteady vocation. Having heard the local Superior's reports, she gave her instructions: to per-suade them to go home and enjoy their native air; as for the Sister who was doing everything to be sent away, it was best to send her back to her family.

2 The image of Saint Anne.

3 The Superior thought she was pleasing her by sending fresh fish, but the Mother makes it quite clear that the opposite is true.

She gives her opinion on the management of the house and vineyard.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just a line to tell you to answer that Gentleman1 that I am very sorry I cannot accept him as our agent; we have had one for many years and I cannot for the house and vineyard; we shall talk about it;2 but it seems to me that you yourselves must see to everything, and show that you will do it, being, as he says, the owners. Your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 That Gentleman. The letter the Mother is answering and other documents are missing, so it is impossible to know who the gentleman was who asked to manage the vineyard and house at the Parrocchietta.

2 Afterwards we shall talk about it. Nothing is known about this either.

Encouragement, good wishes and blessings for the journey to Sicily.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Just one word in reply to yours, but being in haste I tell you that if you could not leave,1 we must always say: may the Lord's will be done in all things. He surely always does what is best for us.2.

  2. So I wish you a thousand blessings from Heaven, and have a good journey. I hold you and shall hold you close to the Heart of Jesus until I hear that you have arrived.3 Goodbye, your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Sister had expressed her regret at having to put off the journey for eight days because the Italian company's steamer did not sail. Forced to use the French company's ship, they had also had to pay the full fare.

2 One must learn to see his fatherly and provident will in every circumstance.

3 The Sisters were going to Sicily, to Termini Imerese, for a new work. They left on 8 July 1878.

She is pleased with what she has written about the house.

A.M.F.

Dear Daughter,

1. Renew your Vows;2 (and) your letter gave me great pleasure, hearing that all is well, the accounts too. Well done!3 Goodbye, yours in my Dear Crucified One

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The date is deduced from the context and the text.

2 The Sisters in temporary Vows in the community could renew their vows on the feast of Saint Anne.

3 Well done! The encouragement was needed by the Superior, who had held the office for only a few months.

She is well and getting on with her work, writing many letters. She awaits news from Sampierdarena. She may join her in Genoa.

A.M.F.

Dear Benedetta, my daughter,

  1. Today I am really better; the herbal brew has done me real good; yesterday I began writing from morning till evening, and today even more! And with my head completely clear! God be blessed, so I am making the most of it to write, for, you know, I was so far behind.

  2. Your letter yesterday was a real comfort to me;2 now I am waiting for news from S. P. d'Arena; but you could well have told Fr Accinelli everything, for indeed he would have taken part and so made sure that the one doing the harm is that Priest.3 Find out why he goes there.

  3. For the rest, don't worry: I am well and doing nothing. Father Agostino is not coming until the end of the week.4 Greet Carla and Gaspare for me, and many kisses to the Little Doll and the nurse; enjoy yourselves.

4. I am tempted to come; if I finish, I shall come. Today I hope to finish sending out the circulars,5 and then I think I would come. The Bishop has fixed 5 August; everything was settled yesterday;6 so you see I may well come. Don't send me any more brew, that is enough now; I still have a bottle.

Goodbye, yours for all ages

affectionate M. Rosa

1 It was classed among the August letters, but it belongs to July, as appears from Sr. A. Benedetta's correspondence and the content of the Mother's July letters.

2 On 13 July she had given her excellent news of her health and of the first benefits of the baths for Carlotta, the Little Doll and herself.

3 Fr Accinelli helped with the good running of the houses in Genoa and Liguria. The name of the Priest is not known.

4 Fr Agostino Donadio used to go to Sampierdarena in summer for sea bathing.

5Cf. L 100.

6 Bishop G. B. Scalabrini was to preach the spiritual exercises, so arrangements had been made with him. Cf. L 102,3.

Various notices: about the Exercises, the feast of Saint Anne and other needs.

A.M.F. Superior,

  1. I inform you that on 5 August the Exercises for Superiors begin here at the Mother House; so be here the day before. Try to join the superior nearest you so as to travel together.

  2. Before leaving, put in your place the sister you think most capable, and tell the sisters in my name to obey her in your absence as they would obey you. Give the sister you leave whatever instructions you think fit so that she runs the house well. Bring the half-yearly accounts with you.

  3. Keep the feast of the Holy Mother on her day, that is the 26th, and do not take the liberty of moving it;2 no one may be invited to dinner, neither confessor nor chaplain: no one, no one.3

  4. You may leave Sr. A. Restilde for 4 August,4 for I hear she is doing well and I rejoice immensely, and you can come down with any postulant you truly see can be accepted. The others can stay at Terricciola, which I think makes four, including Sr. A. Restilde. If there were more, you can take one to Florence.5

M. Sr. A. Rosa

5. Those who have completed a year since their clothing are permitted to renew their vows and to make them.6 You, my dear daughter, be-

fore coming you will receive another notice from me; otherwise stay put, for there is still much sighing to be done over that house.7 Pray, and goodbye. Your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Cf. L 99,4.

2 In small towns the feast of Saint Anne was sometimes moved to the following Sun-day for pastoral reasons.

3 Enclosure of the refectory was the rule. Up to this point the letter is in the secretary's hand. Further notices follow in the Mother's own hand.

4 You may leave... Florence. This passage was added in M. Rosa's own hand to the circular L addressed to Costanza Cenni, then at Terricciola collecting alms. Sr. A. Restilde Colombo belonged to that community.

5 If there were more, send them to Florence, because at Terricciola there was room for only 4 people.

6 Are permitted... M. Sr. A. Rosa. As above in n. 4, in the L to Sr. A. Santina Solenghi. Permitted... to make them: for the first time.

7 ... much sighing. Cf. L 104,4.

She sends her the circular L and a chasuble.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have sent you the chasuble, a very fine one;2 I hope you will be pleased. Greetings to all; I am yours. Read the circular I am sending you. Goodbye,

affectionate M.R.

1 The date is deduced from the context.

2 The chasuble is for the Chapel, which was not yet well furnished.

She asks for news. She misses them but cannot leave headquarters. Their house is being thoroughly cleaned. She is well, has sent off the circulars and is getting through her work.

Dear Carlottina,

  1. Fearing that Sr. A. Benedetta may no longer be there, I am addressing my letters to you. How are you, are you cheerful? And what is Gaspare doing? Tell him his couple of lines were exceedingly dear to me, and he should write and tell me lots of nice things; and the little doll?2 Oh! how long this time seems to me!

  2. Yesterday I said to the Father: "I'm going to Genoa", but he made me see that the time is too short, and so we must be patient.

3. On 5 August the Exercises begin, so even after the Saint's feast it is better for me not to move until everything is over.

  1. Your beds, and the little doll's too, were crawling with bugs as big as bagareni!3 I kept saying: poor little thing! Now they are cleaning them thoroughly and they will not be finished until Thursday. If you could see how well they are doing them! and I have had everything cleaned, and the carpet; in short, you will find everything in order.

  2. I have already sent off all the circulars,4 and nobody helped me. Onorata, apart from Sunday when she had copies made, did nothing else. Yesterday I saw little of her, today nothing yet, but I have nothing to write. One may say the circulars have all gone to their destinations, and I do everything myself.5 I spend the whole morning, from after nine until half past twelve, alone in the study; then in the afternoon I try to tidy something up.

6. I am sending you a little wine by two sisters who are going to Sestri for the baths. If you need anything, write to me.

7. Many kisses to the Little Doll and a thousand things to you two; and if Sr. A. Benedetta is there, tell her to stay and take a few baths, and she will come for the Saint's feast.6 Goodbye. Your

Most affectionate M. Rosa P.S. Father Agostino will come on Thursday or Friday.7

1 Cf. L 99, n. 1.

2 Little doll (Pupetto, Pupa) is the pet name of little Maria Adelaide.

3 bagareni, cockroaches.

4 Cf. L 100.

5 I do everything on my own.

6 For the feast of the Holy Mother, 26 July.

7 Cf. L 99, n. 4.

The big cleaning continues at Carlotta's house. The correspondence is done; she preferred not to go to Genoa because of the heat and lack of time.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Just a line, because yesterday Sr. A. Amabile2 will have told you everything. Listen, the rooms are finished and look really nice; Carla's things are washed and ironed, everything in order; their beds are done, but I am not having them put back until Monday so that they can dry.

  2. The letter half from you and half from Gaspare, you cannot believe how much it pleased me; tomorrow I expect another; it seems a hundred years since I saw the Little Doll and everyone.

  3. As for letters, I have nothing to do; the invitation cards3 are already done; today Onorata was here for half the day but found little work, so much so that we went to listen to the Mass being sung;4 you see I have nothing to do? So be of good heart and take the baths in peace, for they will do your blood good.

  4. I did not come so as not to tire myself, for you know that with the exercises coming I must try not to end up in bed;5 and surely, come to Genoa in this heat? So, God willing, I shall come in September, shan't I?

  5. For the rest, we shall see each other soon. Goodbye; greet everyone for me and give the Little Doll a kiss. I would like the baths to make you as fat as giants. Greet babà,6 Carla, Gaspare.

Your affectionate for all ages

M. Rosa

P.S. Ask Anna Grasso how Florence will end.7

1 Cf. L 99, n. 1.

2 Sr. A. Amabile Montanari, Superior of the Genoa house, had gone to Piacenza.

3 The invitation cards for the feast of Saint Anne.

4 Listen to the Mass being sung. They had attended the singing rehearsals for the Mass of Saint Anne.

5 The exercises were to begin on 5 August. Cf. L 102,3.

6 puppa, babà: pet names for little Maria Adelaide.

7 The Archbishop's order to withdraw the Sisters from Florence had not been revoked. Cf. L 152. She had asked her to pray.

She should ask Mgr Attilio Giovannini how to proceed with the services for the feast of Saint Anne. She should try to find out about the future of the house, which still seems obscure to her and a cause of rumour and gossip-

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Do me the kindness of seeing Mgr Giovannini. I wrote to him and was waiting for an answer, but I see nothing; perhaps I wrote something that displeased him.1

  2. Listen, yesterday they wrote to you to hold a fine service. Before doing the slightest thing, consult Mgr Giovannini and do as he tells you. Never do anything without his consent.2

  3. Alessandro is better; if he doesn't want you to go, so much the better; let him do as he thinks fit. He has a glorious head on him.3

  4. So, for pity's sake, try to find out, because so far there seems to me to be a great deal that is murky. Oh! my God! It really needs a miracle, and the Saint ought to work one for her feast.4

  5. The Cappellone already know everything and are spreading it about. Oh! how sad to see certain persons stoop to the level of gossiping women and make confidences.5 Ah!

6. Let us pray hard, for the Church has great need of it.^6^Goodbye; I am alone; Sr. A. Benedetta is at the baths with Carla, Gaspare and the Little Doll. Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Superior answers her on the 29th, reassuring her: Mgr Giovannini has written to her.

2 Hold a fine service for the feast of Saint Anne. But in Florence the Daughters of Saint Anne had to be careful, because the order to close the house had not been revoked. Cf. L 152.

3 Alessandro did not want visitors and so refused to give his address. Sr. A. Santina had informed the Mother of this.

4 The situation of the FSA in Florence was unclear. Only Saint Anne could intervene with a miracle.

5 The Daughters of Charity have learned of the problem and are talking about it. Certainly some people are behaving like gossiping women, revealing secrets.

6 It is the Church that suffers, because her children give occasion for scan-dal.

All is well.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am getting better and better; for pity's sake take that one away from S. P. d'Arena;2 I cannot wait to hear she is in Genoa. Tell Carla to be cheerful, and Gaspare too. I am writing only to you, because it seems pointless to write three letters.3 No news. Yours for all ages

affectionate M.R.G.

a kiss to the Little Doll

1 The date is deduced from the context.

2 She should transfer at once from Sampierdarena to Genoa the Sister who was not behaving well.

3 Having no news of importance, she sees no point in writing three letters.

She is fairly well and has no reason to tire herself. She asks her to let the Sisters at Sestri know that they may make their vows for Saint Anne's feast, as she has already written to them.

A.M.F.

My more than most dear daughter,

  1. Yesterday I wrote to Gaspare,1 today to you. My health is reasonably good; you know, the usual, which I call good because I am without horrible pains or even headaches.

  2. Don't worry that I am overtiring myself, for I really have nothing to do. The rooms are finished; 2 I don't even look at the church, Sr. A. Costantina does everything;3 as for other matters, I don't know of any, all is quiet.

  3. The Father doesn't even come,4 so I am truly resting; I have little work; you know, most of it is writing, but in that too I am always up to date; in the afternoon there is nothing more to write; the mother-in-law is always at the P..5 and I am in the study alone, alone. Onorata6 comes at half past eleven, stays until two as usual, and then I don't see her again.

  4. So you see I cannot overtire myself; and I beg you not to overtire yourself. Listen, let Sestri know that all are to make their vows, Sr. A. Anacleta,7 all those who have completed a year since their clothing, and I have already written to her. What a nuisance, all this repetition!!! Tiresome! Tiresome! One would have to spend from morning till night answering their nuisances, there being8 so many.

Goodbye, for I want to send it off; greet everyone for me, a kiss to the Little Doll; yours for all ages, my affectionate M. Rosa

2 Cf. L 102,4; 103,1.

2 Cf. L 102,4; 103,1.

3 Sr. A. Costantina Moretti.

4 Fr Tornatore.

5 The mother-in-law. It is not known which Sister the nickname refers to. Always at the p: (the piano?).

6 Onorata Colli helped her with correspondence with outsiders.

7 To Sr. A. Anacleta Marrona.

8 there being, since they are so many.

My daughter,

1. Go ahead and accept the postulants; 1 send them when you think fit, and for the rest you are right that we shall talk in person. So see that they have everything in order, their papers and money.

Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

2. By money I mean what they have decided to let them have,2 and the rest must be secure. Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa
